Answer feedback captures utility beyond retrieval hits.Answer-F1 reward slightly improves
average EM/F1 over graded nDCG, and their mixture gives the best overall answer scores. Answer-
F1 has the highest overall Hit@10 but trails the mixture in EM/F1; graded nDCG and the mixture
also have nearly identical Hit@10 despite different answer scores. Hit@10 counts any answer-
containing top-ten passage and ignores passage order, distracting context, and evidence removed by
the generator’s input limit. Reward choice can thus improve the utility of the generator’s context
even when answer containment changes little.
5 CONCLUSION
RELER aligns embedding models with retrieval and downstream task rewards through vMF explo-
ration in embedding space during training, while retaining deterministic vector retrieval at inference.
Conditional-mean projection removes reward-invisible gradient noise without changing the expected
fixed-candidate gradient. Across BRIGHT backbones, RELER generally improves average retrieval
over InfoNCE, although gains vary by query form and domain. With a fixed document index and
generator, adapting only the query encoder improves both retrieval performance and end-to-end an-
swer quality. These results show the potential of embedding-space RL for retrieval post-training,
and motivate future work on adaptive exploration policies and multi-step retrieval for search agents.

Zero ideal DCG gives zero reward. The pool contains only valid own-query candidates. Teacher
ranks map to gradesℓ m: 3 for rank 1, 2 for ranks 2–5, 1 for ranks 6–10, and 0 otherwise. The main
reward isR nDCG +λR pair withλ= 0.5. The pairwise term averages a score of 1 for a positive
ranked above a negative,1/2for a tie, and 0 otherwise. Positive membership comes from the original
binary annotations iny, not a threshold on teacher grades. A query with no valid pair receives zero
pairwise reward and remains in the batch average. For binary nDCG and MRR controls, labels
indicate all annotated positives. MRR@10 is the reciprocal rank of the first positive within the top
ten, or zero if none occurs. All rewards are evaluated exactly; no differentiable rank relaxation is
used.
Exploration and discrete feedback.For the retrieval rewards used by RELER, changing embed-
dings provides feedback only when it changes a reward-relevant ordering. If every pairing in the
reward table has the same value, all marginal and cellwise LOO weights vanish. Both RLOO and
CMP then give zero updates for that reward component: projection can remove gradient noise but
cannot create a missing reward difference. Concentrating actions too tightly around their means can
make such constant reward tables more frequent; broader exploration changes candidate orderings
more often but can move retrieval behavior farther from deterministic deployment.
RELER uses graded nDCG together with binary pairwise feedback. Graded labels make more swaps
reward-relevant, while an individual positive–negative pair can change order even when nDCG re-
mains constant. The pairwise term can therefore supply feedback in those cases.

C BRIGHT EXPERIMENTS
This section collects the BRIGHT training and evaluation protocol, reference baselines, complete
ablation results, and gradient measurements.
C.1 EXPERIMENTALSETUP
C.1.1 DATA ANDPREPROCESSING
ReasonRank preprocessing removes 133 possible BRIGHT overlaps, 1,546 MS MARCO records, 61
relevance-conflict records, 17 records without negatives, and one duplicate query from 6,721 records.
The remaining 4,963 queries contain 15,830 positive occurrences. Text deduplication preserves all
known positives; annotations and teacher ranks remain separate supervision sources. Source-wise
batching retains 4,896 queries at a per-device batch size of 16, reshuffling within sources each epoch.
Training seeds pair the data order across methods; embedding exploration and negative sampling use
separate random-number streams. There is no internal development split. Overlap screening does
not establish complete semantic decontamination.
C.1.2 REPRESENTATION ANDEVALUATIONSETTINGS
Training and evaluation use the same model and tokenizer initialization. For Qwen3-Embedding, we
reserve one position when truncating text and append a single terminal token, then pool its hidden
state. Last-token pooling, normalization, and similarity computation use FP32. Queries contain a
task instruction followed by the query text; documents use raw text. The backbone uses BF16 during
training and FP16 during evaluation. Training query/document limits are 512/1024 tokens; external
evaluation permits 8192 tokens. Deterministic retrieval uses unscaled cosine similarity.
BGE-M3 uses its dense encoder with CLS pooling, right padding, no appended terminal token, and
no query/document prefixes. Training lengths and the 8192-token evaluation limit follow the same
budget as Qwen3. Its nine training runs use the same prepared ReasonRank data, global batch 128,
113 steps, learning rate5×10 −6, and three seeds as the Q3E-0.6B comparison, with full-encoder
fine-tuning. Only dense retrieval is evaluated; BGE-M3’s other retrieval modes are not used.
Both query settings use the same BRIGHT corpus, relevance labels. 1 For GPT-4 reasoning, we use
the released query field without human-annotated reasoning.

F EXTENDEDRELATEDWORK
Retriever training and learning to rank.Contrastive training underlies dense retrieval and
general-purpose embedding adaptation (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; BehnamGhader
et al., 2024). Learning-to-rank methods complement this representation-learning perspective with
pairwise and listwise surrogates, including differentiable approximations to retrieval metrics (Burges
et al., 2005; Liu, 2009; Taylor et al., 2008; Pobrotyn & Białobrzeski, 2021). Policy gradients have
also been used to optimize retrieval utility through MDP-based ranking policies and stochastic rank-
ings with fairness constraints (Wei et al., 2017; Singh & Joachims, 2019). RELER studies a one-step
embedding action with offline relevance feedback. Its contribution is the continuous policy over
query and document embeddings and its gradient estimator; matched InfoNCE and LambdaLoss
controls assess its value beyond supervised adaptation.
Reward-based retrieval and reasoning.ROPG-RL samples a profile document from a categori-
cal policy over a fixed candidate subset and uses a frozen LLM’s generation metric as reward (Salemi
et al., 2024). RELER’s fixed-index mode instead samples a query vector and searches the full index,
using retrieval or answer feedback in our QA experiments. Retrieval-GRPO updates dense retrieval
using rewards on dynamically retrieved products (Liu et al., 2025c), while Rank-R1 and Search-R1
optimize generated reranking or search-and-reasoning sequences (Zhuang et al., 2025; Jin et al.,
2025a). GRACE optimizes rationale tokens with representation-based rewards and pools rationale-
conditioned states into embeddings (Sun et al., 2026); Embed-RL trains a separate reasoner with
feedback from a frozen multimodal embedder (Jiang et al., 2026). The latter two approaches use
generated reasoning to support retrieval. RELER directly samples query and document embeddings
during training and retains deterministic single-vector inference.
Embedding policies and gradient estimation.vMF distributions also have precedents in hyper-
spherical representation learning (Davidson et al., 2018). REINFORCE baselines, multi-sample
LOO, and product-form recombination are established estimation tools (Williams, 1992; Greensmith
et al., 2004; Kool et al., 2019; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Kuntz et al., 2022). Their use in RELER’s
query and document gradient estimator is detailed in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.1. The closest
antecedent of CMP is document-space projection: Wang et al. (2019) project exploration directions
after interleaved feedback in linear rankers. Our conditional-expectation construction includes vMF
means and accounts for each query–document reward cell and its LOO baseline before updating a
shared encoder. It applies Rao–Blackwell averaging (Casella & Robert, 1996), with a per-term vari-
ance guarantee; variance of the summed encoder gradient is evaluated empirically. The projection
must retain every reward-relevant direction, so the guarantee does not extend to using only returned
full-corpus top-khits.

title: DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex Database Queries
abstract: Recent advancements in large language models have introduced new capabilities for reasoning over structured data, particularly through program-aided tools that can analyze tables. However, many existing methods address single-table scenarios or assume that the relevant tables are already provided. In practice, users often issue complex data exploration queries over entire databases, where relevant information may be distributed across multiple relations. In this work, we introduce DBRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for multi-table question answering. DBRAG first retrieves candidate tables using an offline table index, enriches their summaries with query-relevant rows, and uses an LLM to rerank the candidates. A program-aided reasoner then selects the required tables and executes operations over their full contents, keeping the initial prompt context compact. Experiments on the Spider, GeoQuery, and ATIS datasets used in this study demonstrate improvements in table retrieval and multi-table question answering.
full_text:
DBRAG: Multi-Table Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Complex
Database Queries
Prince Larbi Ampofo Ryoji Kubo Djellel Difallah
NYU Abu Dhabi, UAE
{pla252,ryojikubo,djellel}@nyu.edu
Abstract
Recent advancements in large language models
have introduced new capabilities for reason-
ing over structured data, particularly through
program-aided tools that can analyze tables.
However, many existing methods address
single-table scenarios or assume that the rel-
evant tables are already provided. In prac-
tice, users often issue complex data exploration
queries over entire databases, where relevant
information may be distributed across multiple
relations. In this work, we introduce DBRAG,
a retrieval-augmented generation framework
tailored for multi-table question answering.
DBRAG first retrieves candidate tables using
an offline table index, enriches their summaries
with query-relevant rows, and uses an LLM to
rerank the candidates. A program-aided rea-
soner then selects the required tables and exe-
cutes operations over their full contents, keep-
ing the initial prompt context compact. Ex-
periments on the Spider, GeoQuery, and ATIS
datasets used in this study demonstrate im-
provements in table retrieval and multi-table
question answering.
1 Introduction
Tabular data structures are a widely used data
model for storing information in various domains.
In real-world applications, these tables often con-
tain complex, interrelated data with relational de-
pendencies. When interpreted, relational data can
lead to improved decision-making, enhanced oper-
ational efficiency, and the discovery of new hidden
insights (Fey et al., 2024). Given the inherent com-
plexity of structured query languages, such as SQL,
using natural language can lower the barrier for
data exploration (Li et al., 2024). Consequently,
table question-answering (QA) has emerged as an
important research area focused on developing sys-
tems that can understand natural language queries
and extract relevant insights from tabular data (Jin
et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2025).
Although significant progress has been made in
single-table QA scenarios (Liu et al., 2022; Herzig
et al., 2020; Nan et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2021), the
more challenging and practical task of multi-table
QA remains relatively underexplored. Multi-table
QA involves answering questions that require the
integration of information from multiple tables, ne-
cessitating sophisticated reasoning and advanced
data fusion techniques (Pal et al., 2023). This
challenge is further compounded by the complex
relationships between tables, such as identifying
joinable keys or overlapping attributes, particularly
when such relationships lack a well-structured ex-
plicit relational schema, as is often the case in web
tables and data lakes (Cafarella et al., 2008; Chap-
man et al., 2020).
Many existing studies assume that the relevant
tables are already provided (Chen et al., 2024b; Pal
et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). In an open-domain
table QA setting, the system must instead retrieve
them from a larger corpus. This requires consid-
ering both query-table relevance and table-table
relationships: a table with limited direct relevance
may still be needed to connect complementary in-
formation (Chen et al., 2024a).
Large language models (LLMs) have demon-
strated remarkable proficiency in various natural
language processing tasks (Minaee et al., 2024).
Their adaptation to QA via retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG) has led to substantial perfor-
mance gains (Lewis et al., 2020). In the RAG
framework, relevant information is first efficiently
retrieved from a pre-indexed large corpus and used
to augment the query provided to the LLM, thereby
mitigating issues such as hallucinations and out-
dated knowledge.
Despite the effectiveness of the RAG framework
in single-table QA contexts (Chen et al., 2024b),
its application to multi-table QA remains under-
explored. The challenges of multi-table QA stem
from several factors. First, multi-table QA requires
1
arXiv:2610.07622v1  [cs.IR]  6 Oct 2026
the system to reason across multiple tables, often
necessitating different types of joins and aggrega-
tions. Second, the sheer volume of tables in a typ-
ical database complicates the retrieval process, as
the system must identify not only the main tables
relevant to a query but also any auxiliary tables
needed to connect and augment the data. Third,
each table can vary significantly in size, both in the
number of columns and rows. For instance, data
warehouses often contain wide tables with billions
of rows. These challenges, combined with the lim-
itations of current LLM context windows, make
the direct application of LLMs to multi-table QA
non-trivial, thereby necessitating novel approaches.
To tackle the aforementioned challenges, we pro-
pose a novel methodology that extends the RAG
framework to encompass the entire database. Our
approach decomposes the problem of multi-table
QA into two critical subtasks,multi-table retrieval
andmulti-table reasoning. ➀ In the retrieval step,
we adopt a two-pronged approach to identify the
relevant tables in a scalable manner. First, table
search quickly selects a subset of tables relevant
to the query from the entire database using a table
index. Next, we enrich the tables of interest by
augmenting them with query-relevant rows. The
collected context is then fed into an LLM to se-
lect the most promising tables. ➁ Inmulti-table
reasoning, we propose a novel reasoning protocol
designed to answer the natural language question
given the retrieved tables. Specifically, we design
a multi-table-aware Chain-of-Thought prompting
technique combined with a program-aided reasoner
that executes operations over the retrieved tables
and returns the final answer. Our experiments on
multi-table QA datasets demonstrate that DBRAG
not only improves the retrieval of relevant tables
but also enhances the reasoning task, resulting in
higher overall QA performance in the evaluated
settings.
In summary, we make the following contributions:
⋆ We introduce a RAG approach for multi-table
question answering in settings where the rele-
vant tables must be retrieved from a large table
corpus.
⋆ We propose DBRAG, a novel framework that
decomposes multi-table QA into two subtasks: a
two-stage retrieval strategy that leverages table
indexing and context enrichment, and a multi-
table reasoning protocol that integrates Chain-of-
Thought prompting with program-aided execu-
tion.
⋆ We demonstrate through comprehensive experi-
ments that DBRAG improves both table retrieval
and reasoning performance, resulting in effective
end-to-end QA execution.
ReproducibilityCode, datasets, prompts, rele-
vant parameters, and details of the experimental
setup are available in the project repository:
https://github.com/colab-nyuad/DBRAG
2 Related Work
In this section, we provide a brief overview of
retrieval-augmented generation and then discuss
the most pertinent works on table QA, highlighting
both the inspiration and the novelty of our contri-
butions.
LLMs and RAG.Large language models have
revolutionized natural language processing with
their advanced text comprehension and reasoning
capabilities. However, they are not designed to
handle domain-specific knowledge, rapidly chang-
ing information, private data, or long-tail entities.
These limitations result in issues such as hallu-
cinations (Huang et al., 2025), spurious explana-
tions (Camburu, 2020), and inconsistencies (Elazar
et al., 2021; Adiwardana et al., 2020). Recent tech-
niques have improved reasoning through prompting
methods, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei
et al., 2022) for step-by-step reasoning, and Self-
Consistency (Wang et al., 2023) for selecting the
most consistent answer across sampled reasoning
paths.
To overcome these challenges, recent research
has focused on injecting domain-specific knowl-
edge into language models by integrating external
sources and leveraging domain corpora. Retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG) has proven effective
thanks to a two-stage retrieve-and-read framework,
in which the retriever quickly extracts relevant data
from large corpora (Gao et al., 2023; Fan et al.,
2024). By incorporating accurate, up-to-date infor-
mation, RAG can enhance the LLM’s response per-
tinence, reduce hallucinations, and produce more
reliable, contextually relevant outputs.
Language Models for Table Understanding.
Numerous studies have focused on pretraining
table-specific language models (LMs) for down-
stream tasks. Building on the success of masked
language modeling, TAPAS (Herzig et al., 2020)
introduces a BERT-like architecture enhanced with
positional embeddings to encode table-specific
2
information. During pretraining, the model re-
constructs masked table elements. In contrast to
TAPAS’s reconstruction approach, TAPEX (Liu
et al., 2022) pretrains a language model to execute
SQL operations on tables, motivated by the intu-
ition that accurate SQL execution reflects robust
table comprehension. To advance LM capabilities
in table retrieval, Herzig et al. (2021) develop a
dense retriever leveraging contrastive learning, pre-
training, and negative sample mining. By employ-
ing TAPAS as the base encoder, they demonstrate
that dense retrieval outperforms traditional meth-
ods like BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) in
open-domain single-table retrieval.
LLMs for Single-table QA.Ye et al. (2023) de-
velop a method that enables an LLM to construct
sub-evidences and sub-questions to answer natural
language questions over large tables. Their ap-
proach employs in-context learning by providing
a small set of manually crafted examples to guide
table deconstruction and reasoning. Chen et al.
(2024b) introduce a RAG framework for single-
table QA, retrieving relevant schema and cells to
address scalability and context length limitations
when feeding large tables to the LLM. Inspired by
the effectiveness of reasoning chains in textual con-
texts, Wang et al. (2024) propose using an LLM
agent to dynamically plan table operations based
on prior steps, forming an iterative reasoning pro-
cess. They demonstrate that enabling LLMs to
generate a reasoning chain improves performance
in single-table QA.
Multi-table QA.While single-table QA has gar-
nered research attention, studies on multi-table QA
remain limited. Pal et al. (2023) make a pioneer-
ing contribution by pretraining the TAPEX model
on a multi-table dataset with SQL queries and tab-
ular answers, followed by fine-tuning on natural
language questions. However, their method as-
sumes the relevant tables are already provided to
the model and does not address scenarios where
flattened table representations exceed the model’s
maximum sequence length. Chen et al. (2024a) in-
troduce a method focused on multi-table retrieval,
solving a mixed-integer program that jointly opti-
mizes table-query relevance and table-table rele-
vance. This approach adapts to databases lacking
key-foreign-key constraints. It uses flattened table
representations for coarse-grained retrieval, while
downstream question answering relies on SQL gen-
eration and execution.
3 Methodology
3.1 Motivation and Overview
As mentioned in the introduction, directly present-
ing all tables to an LLM can be expensive and time-
consuming. Additionally, methods that pass com-
plete table information often run into context length
limitations, especially with large tables. To make
matters worse, users issuing ad hoc queries often
do not know which tables are relevant or what the
schema entails. To overcome these challenges and
limit the number of tables presented to the LLM,
we propose an approach that employs a multi-stage
ranking mechanism for efficiency and mitigates
context length issues by summarizing the selected
tables. Additionally, we leverage a prompting tech-
nique that facilitates Chain-of-Thought-style multi-
table reasoning, allowing the LLM to interact pro-
grammatically with the tables. Figure 1 shows an
overview of our proposed framework, DBRAG. In
the following, we begin by formally defining the
setup, followed by descriptions of each component.
3.2 Problem Formulation and Requirements
We formally define the multi-table QA task as
follows. Given a natural language query q and
a databaseD={t 1, t2, . . . , tN}, where each ta-
ble ti is described by a name tName

A standard RAG framework for multi-table QA

rather than a formal diversity guarantee.
(R2) Reasoner Context Size:Full table contents
can exceed the LLM context limit. Compact

3.3 Multi-table Retrieval

Row Index: Context Retrieval.To further en-

4 Experiments
We evaluate our method and baselines focusing on
two key tasks: multi-table retrieval and multi-table
reasoning.
Datasets.Existing tabular QA benchmarks have
largely focused on either limited-domain scenar-
ios or single-table contexts. To address this gap,
MTQA (Pal et al., 2023) introduced a multi-table
QA dataset derived from the cross-domain Spider
dataset (Yu et al., 2018), which spans tables from
138 distinct domains. Their work adapts the origi-
nal text-to-SQL pairs by executing the SQL queries
to obtain tabular answers and excluding examples
with errors or empty results. In our experiments,
we also use the MTQA versions of GeoQuery
(GeoQ; Zelle and Mooney, 1996) and ATIS (Price,
1990; Dahl et al., 1994), two smaller multi-table
QA datasets built on databases of United States
geography and flight booking systems, respectively.
Appendix A details the methodology for construct-
ing the database corpora and the queries. It also
includes a summary of the key statistics of each
dataset.
Experimental Setup and Parameters.In our
method, DBRAG, we utilize GPT-3.5-turbo1 as
the backbone LLM. For efficient dense retrieval,
we employ OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small2
as the encoder fenc. Specifically, we set the coarse-
grained table budget to K= 50 and the fine-
grained table budget toM= 5 , a design choice that
balances precision and recall across diverse user
queries. Unless otherwise specified, the number
of Row Context examples added to the table sum-
maries is set to L= 2 . Additionally, all the LLM-
based experiments are run with a self-consistency
parameter of 5, where we take the majority vote
from five independent runs.

mance. In the following experiments, we focus on
the larger Spider dataset, which presents a more
challenging retrieval setup, and omit GeoQ and
ATIS; their limited number of tables consistently
results in perfect recall across all baselines.

Baselines.Following the work of Chen et al.
(2024a) on table retrieval, we consider the follow-
ing baseline methods:
• Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022): A text re-
trieval method that does not incorporate any table-
specific model design. It ranks tables based on
the cosine similarity between the embeddings of
the question and the flattened tables.
• DTR (Herzig et al., 2021): A method specifi-
cally designed for table retrieval. TAPAS-large
is fine-tuned under this framework, and the rele-
vance of each table to the question is computed
accordingly.
• Coarse-rank: We use our encoder-based coarse
ranking (see Section 3.3) and select the top K=
M= 5 tables, thereby bypassing the LLM-based
fine-grained reranking step.
• JAR (Chen et al., 2024a): This method employs a
base retrieval method and solves a mixed-integer
program to identify relevant tables. We evalu-
ate three versions: (i) JAR (Contriever), (ii) JAR
(DTR), and (iii) JAR (Coarse-rank), which use
the JAR algorithm to rerank the results of Con-
triever, DTR, and our coarse-rank approach, re-
spectively.
DBRAG Ablations.We evaluate several varia-
tions of our method to analyze the contribution of
each component.
• DBRAG (Name and Schema): Modifies the fine-
grained summary so that it includes only the table
name and the table schema.
• DBRAG (Random Rows): Modifies the fine-
grained summary to include the table name, table
schema, and random rows from the table. In this
setup, the LLM-based reranking receives random
rows instead of the relevant rows.
• DBRAG (Relevant Rows): This is our default
setup described in Section 4.
Evaluation Metrics.To assess the quality of
multi-table retrieval, we compare the retrieved ta-
bles against the relevant ground truth tables. Specif-
ically, we use Recall@5 as the metric to evaluate
retrieval performance. Recall@5 measures the pro-
portion of required tables retrieved among the top
five candidates, averaged across queries. For a fair
evaluation, we retrieve the top M= 5 tables from
each method as the set of retrieved tables.

The comparison with Coarse-rank highlights the

4.2 Multi-table Reasoning Performance
Next, we turn our attention to evaluating the end-
to-end performance of multi-table QA encompass-
ing retrieval and reasoning capabilities. In the
following, we use the set of retrieved tables Rq
obtained using DBRAG during the multi-table re-
trieval phase for the three datasets, and feed them
to several baselines.
Baselines.We compare our method against the
following baselines:
• ReadTable (Chen et al., 2024b): This is a com-
mon baseline that embeds the entire table in the
prompt and asks the LLM to solve the problem
using that data. However, if the table exceeds the
model’s context length, the question is marked
as a failure.
• MTQA (Pal et al., 2023): A multi-table reason-
ing baseline that pretrains the TAPEX model on
a multi-table dataset containing SQL queries and
tabular answers, and then fine-tunes it on natural
language questions.
Ablations.We compare our method with the fol-
lowing variations:
• DBRAG (Name and Schema): This setup re-
stricts the table summaries to include only the
table name and schema, without context rows.
• DBRAG (w/o Selection) : Our approach that per-
forms program-aided reasoning without the table-
selection step (Section 3.4).
• DBRAG (Random Rows) : Here, the relevant
rows in the table summaries are replaced with
random rows.
Evaluation Metrics.The performance of multi-
table reasoning is measured by comparing the
ground truth answer table derived from the answer
SQL query with the table generated by the model.
Following Pal et al. (2023), we employ metrics that
determine if the returned table’s features precisely
match those of the ground truth answer.
The evaluation metrics assess table similarity at
different levels of granularity.Table EMmeasures
whether the returned table exactly matches the tar-
get table, requiring both row and column ordering
to be identical; since many queries do not depend
on ordering, additional metrics are used.Row EM
assesses how many rows in the returned table ex-
actly match those in the target table, ignoring row
order but requiring exact value ordering within each
row. Similarly,Column EMevaluates how many
columns in the returned table match those in the
target table, disregarding column order while still
requiring exact value ordering within each column.
Finally,Cell EMprovides the most relaxed evalua-
tion by measuring how many individual cells match
exactly between the two tables.
For Row EM, Column EM, and Cell EM, we
report the macro versions of these metrics to miti-
gate the bias introduced by queries returning large
tables. Statistics about table size and distribution
are provided in Appendix A.

4.3 Varying Table and Row Context Budget
Finally, we evaluate the impact of table and row
context budgets on both table retrieval and reason-
ing performance on the Spider dataset. In the re-
trieval setup (Fig. 2(a)), we vary the coarse-grained
ranking budget K, which determines the number
of retrieved tables provided to the LLM for fine-
grained reranking. Our results indicate that increas-
ing K generally improves retrieval performance
for both approaches, and importantly, the setup us-
ing relevant row context mostly outperforms that
using random row context. For the reasoning setup
(Fig. 2(b)), we vary the number of rows L included
in the table summary. The experiment reveals that
while increasing L initially enhances answer accu-
racy, performance reaches a plateau beyond which
additional rows do not consistently improve per-
formance. This aligns with the intuition that only
a few rows are needed to grasp the structure and
semantics of tabular information. These findings
underscore the effectiveness of compact table sum-
maries in the evaluated setting.

5 Conclusions
We propose DBRAG, a retrieval-augmented gener-
ation framework tailored for multi-table question
answering. DBRAG overcomes the challenges of
complex multi-table relationships by decomposing
the task into efficient table retrieval and multi-table
reasoning. Our approach leverages a two-stage
retrieval strategy, first retrieving candidate tables
from the Table Index and then reranking them using
query-relevant row context, followed by multi-table
chain-of-thought prompting and program-aided ex-
ecution for precise reasoning. Extensive experi-
ments on multi-table QA datasets demonstrate im-
provements in both table retrieval and end-to-end
QA performance. Our results validate DBRAG
as an effective solution for complex, multi-table
database question answering. Future work will
explore further optimizations and extend support
for heterogeneous data integration such as semi-
structured data and knowledge graphs.
8
6 Limitations
Building and maintaining the Row Index can be
computationally expensive for databases with bil-
lions of records. More efficient index construction
and maintenance strategies, including sampling
approaches potentially drawing on the frequency-
based cell selection used by Chen et al. (2024b),
could help address these challenges. We leave these
issues, along with dynamic schema updates and
production deployment, for future work.
While the queries in the datasets involve multiple
tables, their answers can be obtained by executing
SQL queries. In real-world scenarios, however,
users may pose more complex queries, such as
queries for open-ended exploration or interpreta-
tion of trends in the data, which may require analyt-
ical reasoning beyond SQL-based operations (Ma
et al., 2023). The capability of DBRAG to handle
such advanced queries remains unexplored in this
paper.
Additionally, real-world large databases often
present challenges such as noisy data, inconsisten-
cies, and missing information (Hai et al., 2023).
Our method has not been evaluated in these set-
tings, where the model would need to navigate and
address potential flaws in the data itself.
Finally, our comparisons cover a limited set of
baselines for multi-table retrieval and reasoning.
We do not include comparisons with advanced
solvers which could provide further insights into
the performance of our approach.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers) unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposing \emph{AI-decision checkpoints}: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organisational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a \textit{BPM Teaching Case}, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module's output serving as the next module's input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.

AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented

Amin Jalali

Abstract.Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Gen-
eration (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational
business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula
and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-
on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers)
unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-
end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposingAI-decision
checkpoints: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where
process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected
effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organ-
isational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, con-
strain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated
through a fictitious customer onboarding process as aBPM Teaching
Case, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules
that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI
agents, and process mining, with each module’s output serving as the
next module’s input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on in-
structor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps
from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations
suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-
level automation and process-level value.
Key words:BPM education, BPM lifecycle, curriculum design, AI-
augmented BPM, teaching case
1 Introduction
Business Process Management (BPM) is a mature information-systems discipline
that provides concepts, notations, and methods for identifying, modeling, analyz-
ing, redesigning, executing, and monitoring organizational processes [1, 2]. Core
pedagogical content has remained remarkably stable for decades: process discov-
ery and modeling, control-flow analysis, simulation-based performance analysis,
workflow enactment, and process mining [3].
This stability is now challenged by advances in Large Language Models
(LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents. It has become
arXiv:2610.06207v1  [cs.AI]  5 Oct 2026
2 Amin Jalali
technically feasible to introduce AI agents as process participants in knowledge-
intensive tasks [4], such as extracting data from unstructured documents, con-
ducting Know-Your-Customer (KYC) or fraud checks, generating customer com-
munication, and lead generation for claim investigation [5].
Industry adoption of such components currently outpaces their curricular
integration, leaving graduates at risk of two complementary deficits. Classically
trained BPM analysts can model and analyze processes, but struggle to reason
about when and how AI components add value at the process level. Conversely,
AI engineers may be able to build proof-of-concept agents and deploy them in
production but lack the methodological grounding to assess their impact on
end-to-end performance and value creation.
Existing curricular responses tend to follow one of two patterns: appending
a stand-alone module on AI or LLMs to an otherwise unchanged course, or
adding AI-related examples throughout traditional content without altering its
structure. In both cases, AI is treated as a technology topic rather than as a
design concern to be evaluated systematically across the BPM lifecycle.
We contend that the discipline already possesses a suitable backbone for
structuring AI-related reasoning: the BPM lifecycle [1], which has long served as
a textbook spine and didactic organizer. Our contribution is not to propose a new
lifecycle, but to turn the existing one into an active driver of AI-related decision-
making through what we callAI-decision checkpoints: pre-specified points in the
learning trajectory at which students must identify, justify, configure, or reject
an AI component using the analytical instruments of the corresponding lifecycle
phase, transforming the lifecycle from a passive organiser into a sequence of
grounded decision situations. Therefore, this paper makes three contributions:
(C1) It presents a fictitiousBanking casedesigned to sustain multi-module en-
gagement across the BPM lifecycle,
(C2) It introducesAI-decision checkpointsas the organizing pedagogical artifact
of the case, with one checkpoint per lifecycle phase, embedded in a lifecycle-
driven curriculum framework in which each module’s output becomes the
next module’s input across modeling, simulation, redesign, implementation,
and mining,
(C3) It presents aformative reflectionon a Master-level instantiation of the case,
combining instructor observations with insights discovered from the learning-
management-system event logs showing how groups progressed across mod-
ules.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 positions
the work in relation to previous related literature. Section 3 introduces the AI-
decision checkpoint framework and positions each checkpoint within the BPM
lifecycle. Section 4 describes its instantiation in a Master-level course built
around the Banking teaching case. Section 5 reflects on course delivery and stu-
dent performance based on instructor observations and learning-management-
system data. Section 6 concludes and outlines implications for BPM educators
and directions for future work.
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 3
2 Related Work
Despite BPM’s maturity as a discipline, its integration into higher-education cur-
ricula has remained narrower than the scope of professional practice. Moormann
and Bandara [6] issued an early call for action, noting that graduates consis-
tently lack the breadth of skills employers require. To identify related work, a
Scopus search was conducted using the query shown in Table 1, which returned
45 documents at 2026-05-31. After title-and-abstract screening for papers ad-
dressing the intersection of BPM education and AI, three papers were identified
as indirectly related.
On curriculum innovation, Dallavalle et al. [7] propose a PBL-Process Map-
ping Blueprint for undergraduate BPM courses at the University of S˜ ao Paulo,
structured around three next-generation BPM drifts: Conversationality, Auton-
omization, and Sophistication. The blueprint was developed in three phases, cul-
minating in prospective validation through two focus groups with eight alumni.
Participants identified autonomization as the most professionally consequential
drift and called for a brief AI-agent primer to be introduced early in the course.
The blueprint treats AI as one of several emerging competencies to be woven
into existing activities. Our work shares the view that AI must be embedded as a
design concern throughout the lifecycle, but operationalizes it differently: rather
than a primer, we provide students with a structured decision instrument at ev-
ery lifecycle phase, requiring them to justify, configure, or reject AI components
using phase-appropriate evidence.
On teaching cases, Grangel et al. [8] present a teaching case aimed at post-
graduate students in AI, BPM, or Medical Informatics, in which real pseu-
doanonymised clinical data from a Spanish hospital are used to analyse Failure
To Rescue events through process mining and predictive process monitoring.
The case covers process discovery, conformance checking, performance analysis,
and process redesign, and is accompanied by online instructor-facing teaching
notes. Like our Banking case, it grounds BPM competencies in a domain-specific
scenario with real complexity. The key difference is scope: the Grangel et al.
case focuses on applying mining techniques to an existing process, whereas our
case requires students to design, implement, and evaluate AI-augmented process

variants across the full lifecycle, treating governance concerns such as human-
in-the-loop routing and fallback handling as explicit learning objectives.
On LLMs in BPM education, Kluza et al. [9] conduct two experiments in
which ChatGPT-4o and Gemini Flash are tested on typical BPMN assignment
tasks: answering comprehension questions based on five BPMN models (in PNG
and XML format) and detecting errors in 30 flawed BPMN diagrams. The au-
thors conclude that BPMN assignments are not inherently AI-resistant and call
for AI-aware pedagogy in which students learn to critically assess AI-generated
output. In our course, LLMs are not evaluated as assignment solvers but con-
figured and deployed as process participants. The control-flow reasoning limi-
tations that Kluza et al. document are precisely what motivate the AI-decision
checkpoint for implementation, where students must specify schema-constrained
outputs, confidence thresholds, and human escalation paths to compensate for
unreliable AI behavior.
Collectively, these works show that AI is entering BPM curricula through
multiple routes, yet none provides a systematic method for reasoning about
AI adoption across all lifecycle phases using the analytical instruments of each
phase. The AI-decision checkpoint framework addresses this gap.
3 AI-Decision Checkpoints
The proposed framework uses the BPM lifecycle to structure a sequence of
explicit, phase-related decisions about AI adoption. At each checkpoint, stu-
dents contribute to determining how AI can enhance processes by identifying
AI-candidate subprocesses, establishing the baseline, evaluating expected ben-
efits and risks using the analytical instruments of the corresponding lifecycle
phase, and documenting a reasoned decision to adopt, adapt, postpone, or re-
ject specific AI components. This approach decomposes AI adoption from a
monolithic yes/no judgment into a chain of locally grounded assessments that
distribute AI-related reasoning across all phases, anchor decisions in established
BPM instruments, and produce a traceable decision trail that can be revisited.
The framework does not prescribe a correct answer at any checkpoint; it fore-
grounds reasoning quality, requiring students to articulate assumptions, acknowl-
edge trade-offs, and justify decisions. One checkpoint aligns with each lifecycle
phase: identification, discovery, analysis, redesign, implementation, and monitor-
ing [1]; individual checkpoints can be weighted or combined without disrupting
the logic. Fig. 1 positions them relative to the six course modules (M1-M6).
3.1 CP1 - Process Identification: Scoping AI Opportunities
CP1 is located in the process-identification phase. Its purpose is to determine
in which processes and subprocesses AI augmentation is sufficiently promising
to warrant further investigation. The guiding question is:which elements of the
process landscape are plausible AI-candidate subprocesses, and what effects are
they expected to have at the level of entire processes?
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 5
Fig. 1.The BPM lifecycle with six AI-decision checkpoints and their instantiation
in course modules (M1-M6) with associated tool support. We operationalized CP4 in
two modules in our course: an initial simulation-informed redesign in M3 (workflow-net
level) and a final exception-handling redesign in M4 (BPMN level).
The process architecture is examined for subprocesses amenable to AI, specif-
ically those exhibiting high knowledge intensity, data-processing demands, repet-
itiveness, or dependence on scarce expertise. Each candidate’s expected impact
is assessed along thedevil’s quadrangle(time, cost, quality, flexibility) [10], and
risks are cataloged covering legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. GDPR), eth-
ical considerations, data availability, and organizational readiness. The outcome
is an AI opportunity register that combines benefit assessments with initial tech-
nical feasibility in a prioritization matrix, determining which candidates proceed
to later phases.
3.2 CP2 - Process Discovery: Positioning AI in the As-Is Process
CP2 is located in the process-discovery phase. The focus shifts from the process
landscape to a concrete as-is process, and from abstract opportunity identifica-
tion to a precise understanding of how candidates from CP1 relate to existing
organizational work. The guiding question is:given a description of the selected
6 Amin Jalali
process, where would the AI candidates conceptually attach, and which human
and system actors would they interact with or affect?
The as-is process in this phase shall be specified as a normative model and
enriched with an explicit actor perspective. Candidates prioritized in CP1 are
positioned with respect to this model rather than integrated into it. For each
candidate, the analysis specifies (i) the segment of the as-is model it would
conceptually replace, support, or augment, (ii) the human roles and IT systems
currently involved at that segment and how they would be affected, and (iii)
the inputs, outputs, and control transfers currently observed. Escalation paths,
approval steps, and exception-handling mechanisms that would become relevant
under AI augmentation are also sketched at a conceptual level.
The artifact is the as-is process model together with an AI-positioning note
that records, for each candidate, its intended placement, the actors affected, and
prominent structural obstacles or dependencies.
3.3 CP3 - Process Analysis: Performance Baseline
CP3 is located in the process-analysis phase. While CP1 and CP2 establish where
AI augmentation is promising and how it relates to the as-is process, CP3 quanti-
fies the current performance without altering the process structure. The guiding
question is:given an executable representation of the current process, what is the
baseline performance against which any redesign (AI-based or otherwise) must
be assessed?
The baseline can be identified in different ways such as extracting the current
state of the process using process mining, or transforming the model from CP2
into an executable model and simulating the process to identify the baseline. In
courses without prior process data, the latter approach can be feasible; while in
practical settings, other approaches can be followed. Regardless of the method,
the analysis should yield baseline indicators such as average throughput times,
waiting times, resource utilization, and sensitivity to workload variation.
The artifact produced at CP3 is a baseline performance report documenting
the chosen method, underlying assumptions, and key performance indicators,
with particular attention to structural bottlenecks and systematic delays. The
importance is to define a baseline against which upcoming changes can be eval-
uated (whether AI-driven or otherwise). Crucially, where a simulation model is
established as part of this baseline, it serves as a reusable analytical asset: as
redesign proposals emerge in later phases, the model can be refined to reflect the
proposed changes and re-simulated to assess their expected impact before any
real implementation takes place.
3.4 CP4 - Process Redesign: Value-Aware Business Process Redesign
CP4 is located in the process-redesign phase. Building on the baseline from CP3
and the conceptual positioning from CP1 and CP2, it treats AI augmentation
as one design option within a broader redesign effort. The guiding question is:
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 7
when redesign practices are applied, under which conditions does the inclusion
of AI-candidate subprocesses produce to-be process models that outperform the
baseline?
Starting from the executable as-is model and diagnosed weaknesses, the re-
design uses recognized principles (task elimination, resequencing, parallelization,
integration of responsibilities). To-be scenarios include both classical control-flow
and resource changes and variants that embed AI candidates, integrating AI with
redesign moves rather than bolting it on. Redesign variants are distinguished
by the AI technology embedded: (i) LLM-based agents for email intake and
structured data extraction from documents, (ii) RAG-equipped agents for fraud
screening that retrieve and reason over AML rule documents, and (iii) classical
BPM redesign variants without AI components, which serve as the comparison
baseline. All scenarios are simulated under consistent assumptions and compared
to the baseline.
The artifact is a comparative redesign-and-simulation dossier in which each
candidate is assigned a redesign decision, justified by the redesign rationale and
quantitative evidence, including trade-offs such as bottleneck relocation or in-
creased process complexity.
3.5 CP5 - Process Implementation: Realisability and Governance
CP5 is located in the implementation phase and addresses the gap between con-
ceptual redesign and technical realization. The guiding question is:are the AI-
augmented redesign decisions technically realizable within the selected workflow
and AI infrastructure?
The to-be design is mapped onto a concrete workflow platform and inte-
grated with specific AI services, such as LLM APIs or RAG pipelines. For each
AI component, required data flows, performance characteristics, error-handling
mechanisms, and security and privacy constraints are matched against what the
infrastructure can provide. Where the platform does not natively support the
required control-flow patterns or error-handling logic, compensating structures
are introduced, for instance, additional validation activities, schema-constrained
prompts, explicit human approval tasks, or fallback paths triggered on AI failure
or low confidence.
The artifact is an implementation feasibility and governance dossier per AI
component. It records the extent to which the component could be realized as
designed, the workarounds introduced, the governance measures put in place
(logging, thresholds, escalation rules, human-in-the-loop points), and any resid-
ual technical or organizational risks.
3.6 CP6 - Process Monitoring: Mining-Based Insights
CP6 is located in the monitoring-and-controlling phase and concerns the ex-
post evaluation of AI-augmented subprocesses on the basis of execution data.
The guiding question is:given execution data of the deployed process, do the
8 Amin Jalali
AI-augmented subprocesses behave as intended and deliver net value over time,
or should the process be redesigned and reconfigured?
Execution data are collected as event logs once the deployed process has
run sufficiently; in a course setting, pre-generated logs are typically provided.
Process discovery is applied and tested against the normative to-be model from
CP4/CP5; conformance analysis surfaces deviations such as bypassed AI-enabled
subprocesses; and performance analysis quantifies indicators against the CP3
baseline and CP4 simulated expectations. The artifact is a mining-based eval-
uation summary consolidating execution patterns, conformance deviations, and
realized performance. Its insights feed back into CP1, completing the evidence-
based governance cycle.
4 Course Instantiation
The framework was instantiated in a Master ’s-level course for students in the
final year of a Business Information Systems or Computer Science program. The
course has been coordinated by the author for more than 15 years and is designed
based on experience-based learning [11]. No prior knowledge of BPM or AI was
assumed. A total of 152 students enrolled in the course. Of these, 29 had passed
the group assignments in a previous year and were required to participate only
in the individual exam; the remaining 123 were new students who formed 25
project groups, each with a maximum of five members. The course mandates
group work, with results delivered at each module milestone. A key structural
principle is theevolving-artifactorganization: each module’s output becomes
the next module’s input, so students revisit AI-related decisions repeatedly with
accumulating evidence.
4.1 The Banking Case
The primary deliverable of this paper is the Banking case. The six modules (M1-
M6) are built around this case, where students focus on designing a customer
onboarding process comprising customer registration, fraud assessment, and ap-
proval, at a fictitious retail bank facing a scalability crisis. The case is intention-
ally rich in regulatory constraints, knowledge-intensive work, and heterogeneous
data sources, which together make it suitable for realistic AI augmentation sce-
narios. It is structured around two main documents alongside other instructions
distributed to students at different points in the course.
Document A(released at M1, needed for M2) describes the current as-is pro-
cess. Seven roles are involved: a clerk who registers scanned customer requests,
a credit investigator who checks customer credits via an external service, two
CRM officers who manage customer communications and profile activation, an
accounting assistant who enables transactions, and two fraud investigators who
manually review each case against the bank’s anti-money-laundering (AML)
guidebooks. The normal scenario traces a case from registration through credit
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 9
check, parallel profile and account activation, customer notification, fraud re-
view, and either full access or external fraud investigation. A cancellation sce-
nario (needed and can be released at M4) introduces a regulatory constraint on
when a customer can withdraw the case, which is before an external fraud inves-
tigation returns a positive result, requiring a carefully bounded cancel region.
Document B(released at M3) describes the redesign brief: the bank can-
not scale with the current manual process and proposes a combination of AI
agents, where students are guided to prioritize email-based registration ex-
traction and RAG-based fraud screening, as well as web-service automation
(credit checks, profile and transaction management, police reporting). The fraud-
screening agent is deliberately constrained by a known class-imbalance problem
(the data science team reports high recall but imperfect precision), so students
must reason about when the agent’s output can be trusted autonomously and
when a human must remain in the loop.
The hook of the case is established in M1: students build a working proto-
type of the email-intake AI agent before they have modeled the process, then are
asked whether deploying it would actually help the bank. The tension between
“the agent works” and “we don’t yet know if it adds value” motivates the entire
lifecycle journey that follows. Case materials, module instructions, and datasets
are openly available in a GitHub repository 1. Teaching notes, discussion guid-
ance, and sample solutions are available to instructors upon request.
4.2 Module 1 - Process Identification, BPM and AI Foundations,
and CP1
The first module (M1) introduces the conceptual foundations required to apply
the framework: a concise overview of BPM and its evolution, the BPM lifecycle,
and core notions such as processes, subprocesses, and actors, together with an
introduction to the AI technologies most relevant to BPM: Large Language
Models (LLMs), generative AI, and AI agents.
On this basis, the banking case is presented, and students construct a process
architecture for the bank. Within this architecture, they identify AI-candidate
subprocesses, documenting their assumptions as artifacts introduced in CP1. In
the onboarding context, two prominent candidates are expected to emerge from
the given case description: a subprocess handling incoming customer emails and
registration requests (including data extraction from attached documents), and
a subprocess for assessing potential fraud against the bank’s internal guidelines
and regulatory documents.
A complementary lab makes the building blocks tangible: students configure
an AI agent inn8nthat processes customer emails, extracts information from
attached PDF forms using a local LLM (served byOllamato meet on-premises
regulatory constraints), and registers the result into a mock system. The lab
surfaces the distinction between task-level automation and process-level value.
1 https://github.com/jalaliamin/AI-decision-checkpoints/tree/main
10 Amin Jalali
CP1 is discharged by applying the AI opportunity register to the two candi-
dates, yielding a prioritization matrix that determines which proceed to M2.
4.3 Module 2 - Normative As-Is Modeling and CP2
M2 focuses on normative as-is modeling indraw.iousing workflow and pre-
sentation patterns. CP2 is discharged by positioning the CP1 AI candidates
(email-intake and fraud assessment) with respect to the as-is model. Students
also evaluaten8n’s workflow-pattern support from a chief-IT-officer perspective,
producing the AI-positioning note that feeds into M3.
4.4 Module 3 - Process Analysis and Redesign, and CP3 and CP4
M3 covers process analysis and an initial redesign pass. Students transform the
as-is model into a workflow net (WoPeD), verify soundness, configure simulation
parameters, and obtain baseline indicators; performance spectrum analysis in
ProM[12] surfaces bottlenecks. Building on this baseline, students construct and
simulate redesign variants (from classical changes such as task elimination, re-
sequencing, and parallelisation [10] to AI-embedding designs), producing a pre-
liminary CP4 report to be finalized in M4. Splitting CP4 across M3 and M4 is
intentional: the workflow-net redesign grounds design choices analytically before
the BPMN exception-handling redesign in M4.
4.5 Module 4 - BPMN-Centric Process Redesign and CP4
M4 refines the best M3 scenario in BPMN (usingSignavioandTrisotech),
shifting from happy-path to exception-handling redesign. Students apply estab-
lished modeling guidelines to clarify control flow, make subprocess boundaries
explicit, and model human-system-AI interactions and cancellation scenarios.
This enables a second pass on CP4, revisiting AI-augmented subprocess choices
in light of representational clarity and implementability.
The artifact is a consolidated BPMN-based redesign model with clearly iden-
tified AI-augmented subprocesses and associated redesign principles. Together
with the analytical evidence from M3, this model constitutes the final outcome
of CP4 and provides the basis for the feasibility and governance analysis in M5.
4.6 Module 5 - Implementation in Workflow Platforms and CP5
The fifth module (M5) addresses the implementation phase and operationalizes
CP5. Building on the selected and refined BPMN-based to-be model from M4,
students map the preferred redesign onto a concrete AI-augmented workflow in
n8n. The emphasis is on realizing the control-flow structures and subprocess
boundaries defined in BPMN and on technically integrating the AI-augmented
subprocesses retained after CP4.
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 11
Students decompose the BPMN model into an executable workflow and re-
alize AI-augmented subprocesses as concrete agents: an email-intake agent for
document extraction and a RAG-based fraud-assessment agent that retrieves
and reasons over AML rules embedded inQdrant, with a human-in-the-loop
step for flagged cases. The fraud agent introduces students to configuring se-
mantic memory within a workflow platform.
CP5 is discharged by assessing, for each AI-augmented subprocess, the extent
to which the BPMN-level design from M4 can be realized and governed in the
chosen technical environment. The resulting dossier documents (i) alignment be-
tween design and implementation, (ii) workarounds and additional control struc-
tures introduced (validation and enrichment steps, schema-constrained prompts,
fallback paths on AI failure), and (iii) governance and oversight mechanisms. On
this basis, the redesign-level decisions from CP4 are refined into implementation
decisions.
4.7 Module 6 - Process Mining and CP6
M6 instantiates CP6 via process mining. Students receive a multi-year synthetic
event log (constructed to exhibit concept drift). They segment the log, char-
acterize drifts, discover period-specific models, and evaluate them on fitness,
precision, simplicity, and generalization. The artifact is a mining-based evalu-
ation summary consolidating execution patterns, drift evidence, conformance
deviations, and performance indicators that feed back into CP1.
5 Reflection on Course Delivery and Student Performance
The course’s core has been offered by the instructor since 2011; its core scaf-
folding was therefore pedagogically validated prior to the present intervention,
which restructured it around the AI-decision checkpoints and adoptedn8nas the
implementation platform, representing a substantial redesign effort of approxi-
mately 3 months. The course follows a project-based learning (PBL) design [13].
At the time of writing, the exam has not yet been administered, so the evaluation
focuses on group performance in labs and assignments.
Given the single-course, single-instructor design with no comparison group
and no final exam data at the time of writing, all findings below should be read
as a preliminary, exploratory reflection on experience rather than as evidence
of learning effectiveness. The evaluation addresses three questions: (EQ1) Do
students engage with AI adoption as expected phase-specific decision? (EQ2)
How is submission timing distributed across modules, and what does this imply
for course design? (EQ3) How do students perceive the learning value of each
module’s primary activity? Evidence triangulates instructor observations with
insights discovered from LMS event logs extracted by PM4Moodle [14], a vol-
untary end-of-course group survey (conducted per groups), which capture group
interactions at checkpoints. Given the single-instantiation design, findings are
presented as preliminary indications rather than generalizable results.
12 Amin Jalali
Fig. 2.Discovered process map of student-group progression through labs and mile-

Fig. 2 shows a process map discovered with Apromore, using each group

instantaneous as the learning management system only captures the completion

Groups and progression paths:Of 25 registered groups, 24 were active at
the time of analysis; one discontinued after M1. All 24 continuing groups followed
the expected sequential progression, suggesting that the checkpoint artifacts were
sufficient to proceed.
Submission timing and effort distribution:Because the LMS captures
only submission timestamps, module durations are approximated as the interval
from the previous module’s last touchpoint to the current module’s submission.
With this caveat, groups appeared to spent between 9 days and 2 weeks on each
module after M1. This pattern is consistent with student feedback, suggesting
that certain modules should be lightened to reduce overall course density.
Evidence on EQ1 (revised AI assessments):Checkpoint artifacts were
reviewed by the instructor against criteria assessing (i) completeness of the AI
opportunity register or redesign dossier, (ii) quality of justification for AI adop-
tion decisions, and (iii) consistency of reasoning with evidence accumulated in
prior modules. This review was qualitative and based on instructor judgment;
detailed rubrics will be shared in the public repository. To illustrate how check-
points encouraged students to evaluate AI adoption during process develop-
ment, we describe a pattern observed in the CP4 artifacts. Most groups iden-
tified the email-intake and fraud-assessment subprocesses as AI candidates in
CP1 after receiving feedback, and the majority initially expected substantial
reductions in throughput time; in several cases, they estimated that AI-based
intake would halve overall case cycle time. After completing the baseline sim-
ulation in CP3, these groups found that the bottleneck lay not in registration
but in the two-person fraud-investigation queue, which operated near full uti-
lization. Their CP4 comparative redesign dossiers explicitly recorded revised
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 13
assessments: the email-intake agent, while technically functional, was projected
to shift the bottleneck downstream rather than reduce end-to-end cycle time un-
less the fraud-investigation subprocess was redesigned with the help of a second
AI agent equipped with RAG. These groups consequently reclassified the in-
take agent from a high-priority candidate to a medium-priority one, conditional
on redesigning the fraud investigation with the help of an AI agent and apply-
ing a re-sequence pattern to do it earlier in the process. This pattern of initial
overestimation followed by evidence-driven revision was evident in the written
justifications attached to CP4 artifacts and was confirmed through instructor
observations during group supervision sessions. It illustrates the intended func-
tion of the checkpoint chain: not to discourage AI adoption, but to ground it
in process-level evidence accumulated across phases. A comparable pattern of
evidence-driven revision appeared at CP5: several groups that had modeled a
fraud-screening path in BPMN (M4) introduced an explicit human-approval step
in theirn8nimplementation once they encountered the structured-output relia-
bility limitations of the local LLM, converting a conceptual governance require-
ment into a concrete workflow control.
Process identification phase (M1):No dedicated submission point was
designed for students to submit their process architecture and deliverables re-
lated to CP1, as communication for this phase occurred primarily through in-
class presentations. The absence of such a point limits data capture, and we
therefore plan to introduce a dedicated submission box in the next course offer-
ing.
Process discovery phase (M2):Took longer than expected; the cancel-
region pattern proved demanding and will be deferred to M4 in the next offer-
ing. Most groups also postponed formal submissions until the deadline despite
completing labs early; future offerings will require submission immediately after
group presentations.
Process analysis and redesign (M3):Took 1.8 weeks, in line with ex-
pectations. Applying redesign patterns consumed most effort; re-simulation after
model changes proceeded quickly.ProMperformance spectrum analysis required
more time thanWoPeD’s built-in KPIs.
Process redesign using BPMN (M4):Took 1.7 weeks, as expected. Stu-
dents needed to recap cancellation patterns introduced in M2; deferring those
to M4 (planned for next offering) should reduce this overhead. Despite this, stu-
dents engaged more purposefully with exception-handling patterns once their
practical role in redesign was apparent.
Implementation phase (M5):Students completed M5 faster than the
expected two weeks, attributed to cumulative scaffolding: they had already built
an AI agent (M1), evaluatedn8n’s pattern support (M2), and modeled agent
roles and exception paths (M3–M4). Prior checkpoints appeared to pay off at
implementation time.
Process monitoring and mining phase (M6):This module proceeded
as expected; on average, students submitted both the assignment and the lab
within 9 days.

5.1 Threats to Validity and Limitations
Several limitations bound the interpretation of the findings above and warrant
explicit discussion.
Internal validity:The reflections rely on a single instantiation of the frame-
work delivered by the authors. Researcher-instructor overlap may have shaped
both the design and the interpretation of student behavior, even though triangu-
lation with LMS event logs partially mitigates this risk. Furthermore, the course
is still in progress, and individual learning outcomes via the final exam have not
yet been assessed.
2 https://github.com/jalaliamin/AI-decision-checkpoints/blob/main/
Survey_Questions.md
AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management 15
Construct validity:The LMS captures only those interactions that occur
at the predefined touchpoints. Cognitive work conducted outside the LMS (peer
discussion, off-platform prototyping, or iterative refinement of models) is not
directly observable and is approximated indirectly through artifact submissions
and teaching-team observations [15]. The artifacts produced at each checkpoint
also vary in granularity, which constrains comparability across phases.
External validity:The framework was instantiated in a single Master-level
program with a banking onboarding case. While the case is intentionally rich in
regulatory constraints and heterogeneous data, generalization to other domains,
study levels, or institutional contexts requires further evidence. The choice of
supporting tools (draw.io,WoPeD,ProM,Celonis,Signavio,Trisotech,n8n,
Ollama,Qdrant) is opinionated and may affect transferability.
6 Conclusion
This paper presented the Banking case and the AI-decision checkpoint frame-
work that structures it. Six checkpoints, one per BPM lifecycle phase, turn the
lifecycle from a passive organizer into a chain of evidence-grounded decisions
about AI adoption, instantiated in a Master-level course with a continuously
evolving banking onboarding artifact.
Formative evidence suggests three preliminary conclusions. First, checkpoints
appeared to encourage students to treat AI as conditional on process-level value:
groups revised initial over-estimates once simulation evidence accumulated, and
incorporated governance structures in their BPMN and implementation artifacts.
Second, the discovered process map from LMS’s log characterizes submission-
timing patterns and highlights two actionable adjustments: deferring cancella-
tion patterns to M4 and adding a CP1 submission touchpoint for systematic
data capture. Third, a voluntary group survey (10 of 24 groups) indicates that
students perceived positive learning value across all modules (all medians≥4),
with M5 implementation activities receiving the highest ratings, consistent with
the LMS evidence that prior checkpoints appeared to have effectively scaffolded
that phase.
For educators, the framework integrates AI into existing BPM courses with-
out replacing the lifecycle backbone or mandating specific tools. The key trans-
ferable principle is theevolving-artifactstructure, which ensures students revisit
AI decisions with accumulating evidence rather than treating each module as an
independent exercise. Future work will extend LMS instrumentation for richer
data capture per checkpoint and, after several course runs, codify recurrent rea-
soning patterns into structured checkpoint templates to support adoption in
other institutional contexts.

title: Bounded Provisional Visibility: Controlling Poisoning Exposure in Continuously Ingested RAG Vector Stores
abstract: Continuous ingestion can expose new retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) content to retrieval before vetting completes, creating a temporal attack surface that conventional admission decisions do not capture. We present a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol that admits new content under a deadline, hides items whose verification has not committed in time, and supports lineage-scoped containment. The protocol bounds unvetted exposure by the configured visibility budget plus query-path enforcement delay; poisoning exposure remains conditional on verifier correctness. We evaluate the design on five workloads of encoded natural-language documents using an exact backend and Milvus. Under verifier backlog, the deadline reduced median poisoned retrievals from 34 (29--34) to 7 (6--7) relative to asynchronous admission without a deadline, with the same reduction in displaced clean results. Verify-before-visible avoided provisional exposure but delayed clean first visibility to 6.3 s, whereas provisional admission made content visible within 3 ms; expired clean items could nevertheless experience temporary availability gaps. Replaying decisions from a recipe-specific detector illustrated the protocol boundary: false promotions left poison visible, while false refusals excluded clean content from retrieval. Standalone Milvus tests characterized enforcement delay and concurrent HNSW retrieval on one node. These results clarify which guarantees come from the protocol and which outcomes depend on detector quality, while quantifying the freshness and availability trade-offs.

Abstract—Continuous ingestion can expose new retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG) content to retrieval before vetting
completes, creating a temporal attack surface that conventional
admission decisions do not capture. We present a fail-closed
provisional-visibility protocol that admits new content under a
deadline, hides items whose veriﬁcation has not committed in
time, and supports lineage-scoped containment. The protocol
bounds unvetted exposure by the conﬁgured visibility budget
plus query-path enforcement delay; poisoning exposure remains
conditional on veriﬁer correctness. We evaluate the design on
ﬁve workloads of encoded natural-language documents using an
exact backend and Milvus. Under veriﬁer backlog, the deadline
reduced median poisoned retrievals from 34 (29–34) to 7 (6–7)
relative to asynchronous admission without a deadline, with the
same reduction in displaced clean results. V erify-before-visible
avoided provisional exposure but delayed clean ﬁrst visibility to
6.3 s, whereas provisional admission made content visible within
3 ms; expired clean items could nevertheless experience tempo-
rary availability gaps. Replaying decisions from a recipe-speciﬁc
detector illustrated the protocol boundary: false promotions left
poison visible, while false refusals excluded clean content from
retrieval. Standalone Milvus tests characterized enforcement
delay and concurrent HNSW retrieval on one node. These results
clarify which guarantees come from the protocol and which
outcomes depend on detector quality, while quantifying the
freshness and availability trade-offs.
Index Terms —stream ingestion, admission control, systems
security, retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, data
poisoning
I. I NTRODUCTION
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a language
model’s output on documents retrieved from an external
knowledge base [1], and dense passage retrieval turns that
lookup into embedding-similarity search, commonly served by
a vector store [2]. As deployments move from static corpora
to live knowledge, that store must absorb new content while
serving queries.
Streaming RAG refreshes the knowledge base as content
arrives [3], while versioned vector lakes retain temporal views
over continuous updates [4]. Both aim to reduce freshness
delay. Low freshness delay and trust assessment are in ten-
sion: establishing that a newly arrived item is trustworthy
takes time because it requires checking provenance, scanning
for adversarial or promotional manipulation, and comparing
against existing knowledge. A freshness objective instead
pushes the same item toward the query path as soon as
possible. Systems with aggressive freshness objectives may
therefore permit provisional content to become query-visible
before veriﬁcation completes. This is a design option, not a
requirement: keeping unveriﬁed content invisible until fully
vetted avoids unvetted exposure at the cost of veriﬁcation-
dependent freshness delay, a policy we retain as a baseline. We
study the security consequences of the low-latency operating
point and how to constrain them.
Admitting content before it is vetted creates an exposure
interval. Corpus-poisoning attacks can steer dense retrievers
with a small injected set, including for unseen queries [5],
and PoisonedRAG further shows that a few injected texts
can induce attacker-chosen answers in an end-to-end RAG
pipeline [6]. In a continuously ingested store, that exposure
is fundamentally temporal: a provisionally admitted poisoned
vector can be retrieved throughout the window between ﬁrst
visibility and containment, whether or not a detector eventually
ﬂags it.
This temporal systems view falls between existing lines:
poisoning defenses report detection effectiveness on static or
batch-constructed knowledge bases, and continuously updated
vector stores are mature but security-agnostic (Sec. VIII).
We present a fail-closed provisional-visibility protocol for
streaming vector stores. New content is query-visible but
bounded by a conﬁgurable visibility deadline Tp; only positive
multi-signal veriﬁcation promotes an item; expiry hides it
instead. A deadline scheduler decoupled from the veriﬁca-
tion queue makes that guarantee survive veriﬁer backlog,
and content later found malicious is excluded from retrieval
by lineage-scoped containment without rebuilding the store.
