Sweeping Tp exposes a measurable trade-off between freshness
and exposure.
This paper makes four contributions. C1 (Formalization).
We deﬁne unvetted exposure Eu, poisoning exposure Ep,
containment, and recovery as distinct intervals, separating
what a protocol can guarantee ( Eu) from what depends on
detector quality ( Ep). C2 (Protocol). We design a fail-closed
provisional-visibility protocol whose invariants I1–I7 guaran-
tee that unveriﬁed content cannot remain query-visible beyond
Tp + δhide and that each item is provisionally visible at most
once. A metadata time-to-live alone does not give this: an
expiry that queues behind the veriﬁer inherits its backlog.
C3 (Containment). We implement lineage-scoped containment
that excludes a compromised item’s descendants from the
query path before physical purging completes, and measure
its collateral revocation. C4 (Evaluation). We quantify dead-
line effectiveness and clean-content cost, evaluate a recipe-
speciﬁc feasibility detector and replay its decisions through
the promotion path, characterize eligibility completeness, and
evaluate δhide and hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW)
behavior on standalone Milvus.
II. B ACKGROUND AND THREAT MODEL
A RAG pipeline embeds a query, retrieves the top- k nearest
chunks from a vector store and conditions generation on
them; under continuous ingestion an upstream stream is
chunked, embedded and inserted while queries are served.
We model the store as an insert path and a query path that
observe a per-item visibility state.
A. Threat model
We assume an adversary who can submit content into the
ingestion stream or control an already-authorized source. The
adversary may optimize against the retriever and any known
lightweight admission signal. Prior work shows high attack
success from a few retrieval-targeted texts [6]; SilentRetrieval
further demonstrates a ﬂuency-constrained evasive variant [7].
Injection is at a bounded rate (0.1–5% of the stream), steady
or bursty, with retrieval results observable. A poisoned item
succeeds if it is retrieved for a target query before it is
contained.
The adversary cannot modify admission metadata, the
deadline scheduler, per-item visibility state, or provenance
records; fully compromised veriﬁers, a malicious control-plane
operator, and embedding-model backdoors are out of scope.
We do admit trusted-source compromise: an item may carry
valid provenance yet be malicious. In RAGShield’s numerical-
claim setting, an insider with valid signing credentials reduces
provenance-only admission to the no-defense attack-success
rate [8]. We therefore do not rely on provenance alone for
promotion (Sec. IV -C).
B. Scope
We defend the ingestion-to-retrieval lifecycle of a single
vector-store deployment as observed through its supported
query path; the detector/veriﬁer is a pluggable component
throughout. Strict multi-replica/cache consistency and fully
distributed rollback are out of scope (Sec. IX).
III. P ROBLEM FORMALIZATION
For an ingested item x we distinguish the lifecycle times-
tamps tarrive, tvisible (ﬁrst retrievable through the supported
query path), tdetect, tcontain (no longer returned by the query
path), tpurge (physically deleted from the live store) and
taudit. The visibility deadline is anchored to ﬁrst visibility,
tdeadline = tvisible + Tp; anchoring to arrival instead shifts Eu
by the small admission-to-visibility gap. Freshness delay is
D f = tvisible − tarrive and recovery is Wrecovery = tpurge − tdetect;
physical live-store purge is treated separately from logical
containment.
We deﬁne unvetted exposure as the interval during which
unveriﬁed content is query-visible, with both endpoints on
the query path: Eu(x) = tqp-exit(x) − tvisible(x), where tqp-exit is
when the path stops returning x as unvetted, after promotion,
rejection or expiry. We deﬁne poisoning exposure as the
interval during which a malicious item can inﬂuence retrieval,
Ep(x) = tcontain(x) − tﬁrst-poison-visible(x); it depends on detector
false negatives and promotion policy, so the protocol bounds
it only when the veriﬁer never falsely promotes. We deﬁne
enforcement delay to record that a metadata state change is
not containment until the query path honors it: with texpire the
deadline instant and tqp-hide the moment the query path stops
returning x, δhide(x) = tqp-hide(x) − texpire(x).
The guarantee has three layers. (i) Operational bound.
Expiry ﬁres at tvisible + Tp whatever the veriﬁer is doing,
because the scheduler does not share its queue, and the query
path stops returning the item δhide later:
Eu(x) ≤ Tp(x) +δhide(x). (1)
Only query-path visibility counts, so exposure ends at tqp-hide
rather than at the earlier control-plane transition; anchoring
there would put δhide outside the interval and make (1) true by
arithmetic. Equation (1) separates the conﬁgured deadline from
a deployment-speciﬁc enforcement slack. The latter comprises
scheduler ﬁring, state commit, and query-path propagation
(Sec. VI-A); each is ﬁnite only while the control plane is
live, so operators must provision and monitor δhide. The
protocol makes that term independent of veriﬁer backlog: a
separate scheduler and an O(1) ﬂag write provide it, although
shared-resource contention can still affect its magnitude. (ii)
Conditional poison bound. For a malicious item never falsely
promoted, the same bound applies to Ep. (iii) General case.
After false promotion, exposure is governed by detector error
and later containment. We therefore retain an oracle arm as a
mechanism upper bound and separately evaluate one recipe-
speciﬁc detector and its lifecycle consequences (Sec. VII).

B. Item state machine
Fig. 1 gives the atomic compare-and-set transitions; com-
peting veriﬁcation and deadline events are ordered by commit
time (Sec. IV -D).
C. Positive veriﬁcation and hard gates
Promotion requires afﬁrmative decisions from noncompen-
sating source/integrity ( S) and content/behavior ( C) families;
C is mandatory under trusted-source compromise. D1 instan-
tiates this contract. The S family checks credential validity,
provenance consistency and the pinned encoder revision. The
C family sums calibration-standardized half-passage cosine
repetition and distance to the ten nearest corpus posts af-
ter excluding the item’s source group. Its threshold 1.3553
maximized poison-class F1 on 448 calibration groups, then
remained ﬁxed for a single evaluation on 512 disjoint test
groups; D1 received neither test labels nor evaluation queries.
Only the content family contributes detector-quality evidence;
the source-family controls validate interface plumbing.
D. Deadline enforcement and atomic transitions
Fail-closed enforcement rests on decoupling. A dedicated
scheduler, driven by per-item deadlines and independent of
the veriﬁer queue, performs expiration; hiding is an O(1)
visibility-state transition honored by the query path through
the authoritative ﬂag, waiting neither for veriﬁcation nor for
physical deletion. The enforcement delay δhide therefore does
not queue behind the veriﬁer, the property on which (1) rests
under load.
Because a deadline and a veriﬁcation result may occur con-
currently, all transitions are atomic compare-and-set operations
conditioned on the current state, and the race is resolved
by commit time: a promotion succeeds only if the item is
still PROVISIONAL and the positive veriﬁcation committed
no later than the deadline; otherwise the scheduler commits
PROVISIONAL → HIDDEN and a late positive result com-
mits HIDDEN → TRUSTED idempotently. A veriﬁcation that
ﬁnishes computing before the deadline but commits after it
is thus post-deadline, so a veriﬁer cannot use its internal
completion time to extend visibility.
E. Lineage-scoped containment and recovery
Each vector carries lineage metadata: document ID, source
and version, ingestion batch, embedding-model version, chunk
parent, and vector ID. A trusted item is revoked following
a later veriﬁer alert or a source/lineage revocation event,
such as a credential judged compromised or a batch ﬂagged
by an operator. Continuous per-item large language model
(LLM) monitoring is out of scope. Containment revokes
only the affected lineage rather than rebuilding the store.
Operationally, operators should choose the narrowest scope
the alert evidence justiﬁes: source scope for a compromised
publisher or credential, batch or version scope for a suspect
ingestion unit, and item scope only when the affected object
is localized and lineage is reliable. A scope narrower than
the evidence may leave correlated descendants visible, while
a broader one increases clean collateral removal. Logical
containment, an O(1) exclusion, occurs when the supported
query path no longer returns the item and ends measured poi-
soning exposure ( tcontain); physical live-store purge is deﬁned
separately through recovery latency ( Wrecovery), so a security
metric is not conﬂated with database garbage collection. The
query-path guarantee establishes exclusion rather than erasure.
Operationally, before live-store purge completes, a hidden
vector may still occupy index storage; snapshots or exports can
preserve it afterward. Revocation tombstones must therefore be
retained and honored during restore and rebuild for as long as
such copies exist. Access control and audit remain necessary
until all retained copies are deleted.
F . Protocol invariants
Each invariant maps to a tested property. I1–I2 require
afﬁrmative S and C decisions with no hard-gate failure; the
oracle tests the promotion outcome and D1 the concrete
decision path. I3 makes expiry hide, I4 enforces (1), I5
ends exposure at logical containment, I6 decouples expiry
from veriﬁcation and deletion, and I7 permits one provisional
episode. Lifecycle invariants I3–I7 run in both arms. A risk-
dependent Tp(x) = f (r(x)) changes none of them.
V. I MPLEMENTATION
We implement the control plane on a streaming vector-
store stack. Content arrives through an asynchronous ingestion
producer and is routed by an admission service that applies
the cheap hard gate and assigns the visibility deadline, then
inserts admitted items into a single Milvus [9] collection.
PROVISIONAL and TRUSTED are eligibility states in the
control store rather than separate collections: promotion ﬂips
state and moves no vector, and the query service serves both
under one top- k (Sec. IV -A).
The authoritative item metadata (visibility state, deadline,
lineage, and audit timestamps) lives in a separate lightweight
control store, not in the vector database, which holds vectors
and serves retrieval while the query service decides eligibility.
Manu retains row-level ACID while explicitly relaxing com-
plex transaction requirements for vector workloads [10]. Our
protocol needs atomic transitions over those ﬁelds, so they
remain in the control store. Under post-ﬁltering, updating the
visibility ﬂag is an O(1) write that the query path honors im-
mediately and that is decoupled from deletion or compaction.
The timer-ordered scheduler does not share the veriﬁer pool;
together, these two forms of decoupling realize I6. Transitions
are compare-and-set updates (Sec. IV -D), and lineage columns
enable scoped revocation without a rebuild.
The veriﬁer interface has two instantiations. A deterministic
oracle isolates lifecycle timing; the detector arm replays held-
out D1 decisions and measured detector-only service times
through the same promotion path. It therefore captures ob-
served errors and latency but excludes online detector and
model contention. A single-process in-memory harness val-
idates the control plane without noise. The same interface can
be backed by a real vector store. Section VI-C compares the
resulting post-retrieval eligibility check with an in-index ﬁlter.
The harness, preregistrations and authoritative result ﬁles are
available from the authors, each recording the runtime-code
ﬁngerprint it was produced under.
VI. E VALUATION SETUP
We ask whether Eu is bounded and how much the enforce-
ment delay δhide widens it; whether that bound survives veriﬁer
overload; how freshness trades against exposure over Tp; what
top-k completeness cost eligibility enforcement imposes; and
how precise containment is. A separate experiment reports
HNSW index ﬁdelity [11] and descriptive single-node through-
put and tail latency across ﬁve independently restarted Milvus
Standalone processes (Sec. VII-G).
A. Instrumentation and derived metrics
Every lifecycle metric derives from one versioned event
schema of per-item timestamps, so the standalone deployment
emits the same ﬁelds without changing a deﬁnition. Three
distinctions matter. (i) tverify-end ̸= tverify-commit: a result com-
mitted after the deadline is post-deadline (Sec. IV -D). (ii)
Scheduler ﬁring, state commit and query-path propagation are
components of δhide, not extra terms in (1); observed through
probes, it is interval-censored, so we report the conservative
upper bound and never charge the probe interval to system
delay. (iii) Per-query item state is logged as observed at return
time, never reconstructed from the item’s later state, which is
what the residual exposure rate depends on.
B. Workloads, baselines, and parameters
Four workload classes stress different facets: ingestion un-

exercising I6, and post-promotion revocation. Each poison-
burst workload is generated from scratch: an eight-topic corpus
of 600 unit vectors, eight queries from the attacked topic
for crafting and eight more, disjoint, for measurement, eight
from other topics as controls, and six poison vectors perturbed
toward the crafting queries alone. Queries are issued at a ﬁxed
rate over a ﬁxed window with the poison injected partway
in, using ﬁve ﬁxed seeds, all retained. Four baselines share
one ingestion path and differ only in admission policy: B1

C. Eligibility enforcement
A post-retrieval authoritative check (post-ﬁlter) and an in-
index metadata ﬁlter trade off along three axes: δhide, query
latency, and retrieval completeness. Post-ﬁltering gives a small
δhide because the control store is authoritative, but it ﬁlters after
approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search, so it can under-
ﬁll the top- k; the in-index ﬁlter avoids under-ﬁll but its hide
observability is left to the store’s read-consistency level [10],
which we ﬁx and report. With α over-fetch and pool size
M = αk, post-ﬁltering under-ﬁlls exactly when pool hidden
occupancy hM(q) exceeds 1 −1/α, so under-ﬁll is governed by
the upper tail of hM and not its mean. We therefore vary three
hidden distributions: uniform-random, semantic-clustered, and
query-coupled. The query-coupled set is built with knowledge
of the evaluation queries, so it is a worst case by construction;
the eligible population stays ≥ k, so exact ground truth stays
well deﬁned. Completeness is reported as under-ﬁll (result
count < k) and Eligible Recall@ k against exact brute-force
ground truth, plus Conditional Recall@ k given a full- k result,
which isolates ANN approximation error.
D. Invariant validation and reporting
Automated tests assert that timeout never promotes, that
each item enters PROVISIONAL at most once, that a post-
deadline-committed pass ﬁres HIDDEN → TRUSTED rather
than PROVISIONAL → TRUSTED, that HIDDEN and RE-
VOKED items are never returned, and that logical containment
holds while physical purge is pending. An overload test injects
heavy veriﬁer backlog and conﬁrms unvetted items still leave
the visible set within Tp + δhide.
VII. R ESULTS
The exact and Milvus Lite tiers validate lifecycle mechanics
and eligible ground truth; D1 adds measured decisions, and
Standalone adds HNSW with 1–16-client load.
A. Deadline enforcement under veriﬁcation backlog
The harness validates invariants I1–I7 and the commit-time
rule (20/20 checks). The real-time functional slice runs the full
ingest → provisional → deadline → hide → late-verify →
trusted → revoke lifecycle with 8/8 checks in both eligibility
modes. Decoupling the scheduler from veriﬁcation is what
bounds unvetted exposure under backlog: under 50 × backlog,
decoupled scheduling gave Eu ≈ Tp versus 50 Tp under coupled
scheduling. On the Milvus Lite real-time control plane, Eu was
1.00 Tp decoupled versus ≈5 Tp coupled under a ∼5 s backlog.
B. Retrieval-layer poisoning exposure and clean-content cost
Poison crafted against a designated query set is injected
into a collection held loaded throughout, with eligibility on
the post-ﬁlter path, and we measure what each baseline lets
it do (Fig. 2): ﬁve independently generated workloads whose
synthetic corpora keep exact eligible-neighbor ground truth
computable; Sec. VII-C repeats the grid on encoded natural-
language documents. Three query sets separate what one
poisoned-retrieval rate conﬂates. The set Qcraft, the queries the
poison was optimized against, is a worst case by construction;
Qtgt holds disjoint queries of the same topic, so a hit there is
transfer; Qneg is unrelated. Rates are reported over the queries
B1 compromised, a set applied unchanged to every baseline
and Tp; counts are unaffected by that conditioning.
The poison reached 75–100% of crafted queries, while
transfer was partial: it reached 12–38% of disjoint same-
topic queries, with every workload showing some transfer,
and produced no poisoned retrieval on any of the 40 distinct
unrelated queries. Whether a query retrieves poison is decided
by the best poison it can see against its own top-5 cutoff, so
we report that pairing rather than an average over unrelated
pairs: for the median target query the best poison falls 0 .037–
0.061 short of the cutoff, and yet 1–3 of each workload’s eight
queries clear it. Predicted and retrieved agree for every one of
the 80 held-out queries across both workloads (Sec. VII-C),
so the transfer rate is a property of the geometry, not of the
defense or of when a query happened to run.
Under backlog, the deadline rather than veriﬁcation ended
exposure (Table I). B1 never contains the poison; its exposure
window ends only when measurement stops. B3 holds at
B1’s rate for 4 .7 s until veriﬁcation drains, and B4 is cut at
the deadline; the conditional rates are 0 .57–0.63 for B3 and
0.125 for B4, versus 0 .875 for B1. Counts and rates are both
per-workload medians over workloads whose qualiﬁed-query
counts differ, so the rate is not the ratio of the counts. When
the veriﬁer keeps up, the two are indistinguishable, because
veriﬁcation commits inside Tp and the deadline never binds:
the deadline is what makes the bound survive backlog, not
what creates it.

C. Real documents, a real encoder , and poison written as text
A planted geometry cannot establish transfer to a retriever
whose geometry did not deﬁne the attack, so we repeat
the grid of Sec. VII-B with the data replaced; a valida-
tion check conﬁrmed that all timing and protocol parame-
ters were unchanged. The corpus becomes 600 posts from
eight 20 Newsgroups categories spanning recreation, science,
computing, politics, religion and commerce, 75 each, with
headers, footers and quoted replies stripped, encoded by all-
MiniLM-L6-v2 at 384 dimensions; queries are the opening
words of held-out posts, leaving Qcraft and Qtgt disjoint real
utterances. The poison is an English passage inspired by
PoisonedRAG’s black-box query-repetition construction [6]:
our implementation repeats the target query, appends ﬁxed
assertive ﬁller and tests whether the result enters the encoder’s
top-k without manual vector-space placement. It does not
instantiate PoisonedRAG’s target-answer generation condition.
The attack survives the substitution. Judged by the same
per-query top-5 cutoff rule, the poison falls 0 .034–0.093 short
for the median target query, and 1–3 of each workload’s
eight clear it anyway. Poison was retrieved for 12–38% of
these queries, with at least one transfer in every workload,
but for none of the 40 distinct unrelated queries. Prediction
and retrieval agreed for all 40 real and all 40 controlled
queries. Query opportunity was ﬁxed: each query ran eight
times, seven against an unchanged candidate set. Together,
these observations support attributing transfer to the encoded
geometry rather than query opportunity.

129/65/255/63; recall was 125/128 for the matched recipe

D. Eligibility enforcement and top-k completeness
V alues below are means across three seeds; each seed’s
P95, under-ﬁll rate and recall are computed separately before
aggregation. At 30% global hidden occupancy with 2 × over-
fetch, clustered hiding raised the P95 candidate-pool hidden
occupancy from 0 .47 to 0 .58 and under-ﬁll from 0 .7% to 8%
at an unchanged median hM of 0 .30; the query-coupled stress
construction gave 26%. At 1 × over-fetch, Eligible Recall@ k
was 0 .70, 0 .68 and 0 .38 under uniform, clustered and query-

and recall reached 1 .0 in all three. Conditional Recall@ k was

ﬁlter returned the exact eligible top- k wherever the eligible

E. Milvus Lite functional validation
On Milvus Lite, the adapter, all four state paths and both
eligibility modes execute against a real Milvus API and
reproduce the trends above. Conditional Recall@ k was 1.0
because the FLA T index adds no ANN approximation.
F . Lineage-scoped containment
In the evaluated revocation workload, lineage-scoped con-
tainment caught 100% of the poison at all three granularities,
while collateral removal fell from ∼83% (by source) to ∼43%
(by batch) to 0% at exact item-lineage granularity. At equal
poison recall, these ﬁgures quantify the collateral cost of each
scope choice and the reduction in collateral removal when alert
evidence supports a narrower scope; they do not identify a
universally optimal granularity. Through the post-ﬁlter path,
no residual retrieval followed logical revocation on either
backend. Through the in-index path, it persisted immediately
after the scalar update on Milvus Lite ( ∼29–48% of probes),
so that path propagates a hide with nonzero delay (Sec. VI-C).
G. Standalone system results
We ﬁrst conduct a single-run propagation microbenchmark
on Milvus Standalone v2.4.15 (single node, Docker) [9] over a
200-item collection of synthetic unit vectors and measure the
in-index mode’s δhide end to end. The delay δhide is computed
from deadline expiry per the logged timestamps; probing be-
gins at acknowledgment. Two probes run concurrently: a scalar
point lookup and an exact (FLA T) top- k search. FLA T is used
because under an approximate index a vanished item cannot
be distinguished from a recall miss; concurrency keeps either
probe’s service time from being charged to the other. The
grid is four read-consistency levels × {no, heavy} backlog,
Tp = 1 s, 200 hide events per cell, with an identical control cell
at the start and end of the run; we report δhide as a conservative
upper bound derived from interval censoring (Sec. VI-A). The
hide is an override upsert because v2.4.15 has no in-place
scalar update, so the magnitudes are properties of that update
path as well as of the protocol.
Read consistency determined whether completed probes
remained stale after the hide committed. Under Strong and
Session, no completed probe returned the item in any cell: 0
stale reads out of 200 events per cell. Under Bounded and
Eventually, provisional items stayed retrievable across dozens
of completed probes.
In the Bounded and Eventually cells δhide was 288–332 ms
at P50 and 380–431 ms at P95; the 9–12 ms censoring bracket
means that the reported bounds overstate the true delay by at
most ∼12 ms. Under Strong and Session, the probe itself costs
∼420 ms at P95, so the ﬁrst completed probe already reports
the item hidden and δhide is bounded but never point-estimated.
That 420 ms characterizes the instrument, not the underlying
delay, which may be identical across modes. Adding the scalar
probe added no material cost to the top- k search path under
this workload (P95 421.0 ms with it versus 419.7 ms without),
so these delays are not an instrumentation artifact.
Thus δhide must be budgeted: at Tp = 1 s, a P95 enforcement
delay of ∼0.43 s widens the worst-case unvetted-exposure
window by more than 40%. That magnitude belongs to the
in-index scalar-update path, not to the control-store post-ﬁlter
conﬁguration of Sec. VII-B.
The panel cannot identify a veriﬁer-backlog effect. Its two
control cells perform identical query-only work at the run’s
start and end, yet their P50 values differ by 22.3 ms (6.5%), a
shift that exceeds the between-cell effects. We therefore report
rounded magnitudes and categorical behavior only: where δhide
resolved, the backlog contrast changed sign (Bounded +50 ms,
Eventually −23 ms), and both magnitudes were of the same
order as the control drift. With 200 events per cell, the panel
supports median estimation; P95 is tail-limited, and P99 is not
reported.
We report ﬁve Milvus process runs that passed ﬁxed validity
gates; the artifact retains all attempts. Each run built a 100,000-
vector HNSW index using cosine similarity [11], with M = 16,
efConstruction=200, and Strong consistency. Each run
used the same ﬁxed set of 192 queries. At the primary ef=64
setting, run-level median Recall@5 was 0.9979 (range 0.9979–
0.9990), median P95 latency was 0.412 s, and no query errors
occurred. With 20 admissions/s, median throughput across
the four admission policies increased from 3.27–3.33 queries
per second (QPS) at concurrency 1 to 48.0–51.27 QPS at
concurrency 16, with no admission failures. Median P95 query
latency at concurrency 16 was 0.408–0.416 s.
VIII. R ELATED WORK
Corpus-poisoning attacks can steer dense retrieval with a
small injected set [5], and PoisonedRAG extends the threat to
attacker-chosen generation [6]. We propose no new attack.
SilentRetrieval studies ﬂuent, semantics-preserving variants
of such poisoning [7]. Our threat model admits this adversary
(Sec. II-A).
RAGuard ﬁlters suspicious retrieved chunks [12], and PRA-
RAG robustly aggregates retrieved evidence [13].
Orchestration and forensics complement such ﬁltering.
ADO selects defenses per query context [14], and RAGForen-
sics traces harmful outputs to responsible passages [15]. These
studies predominantly use static or batch-constructed corpora
and report method-speciﬁc outcomes rather than temporal ex-
posure, containment and recovery under continuous ingestion.
In-toto formalizes software-supply-chain attestation for how
an artifact was produced [16], and RAGShield applies prove-
nance checks to RAG ingestion and shows their insufﬁciency
against a valid-key insider [8]. The latter result motivates our
multi-signal rule without prescribing a detector.
Milvus provides similarity search over mutable collec-
tions [9], and Manu develops a cloud-native vector-DBMS
architecture [10]. Our control store holds only eligibility state
beside such a system (Sec. V).
FreshDiskANN supports incremental updates of a graph
index [17], while SPFresh performs in-place updates without
full rebuilds [18].
Freshness has also been pursued at the RAG layer. Stream-
ing RAG incrementally refreshes a compact prototype in-
dex [3], and SPI adapts retrieval resolution per query [19].
Temporal retrieval is a further direction. LiveV ectorLake
adds versioned point-in-time retrieval [4]. These systems opti-
mize freshness, update efﬁciency or temporal retrieval but do
not model adversarial exposure windows.
A recent RAG-security survey separates admission-time
integrity, retrieval-time hardening and post-retrieval mitiga-
tion [20]. Our focus is the temporal ingestion-to-retrieval
lifecycle under concurrent updates.
IX. L IMITATIONS
The Eu ≤ Tp + δhide bound inherits the deployment’s en-
forcement delay. The corresponding Ep bound holds only
absent false promotion; falsely promoted items require later
containment. V erify-before-visible avoids provisional exposure
at higher freshness delay, and a deadline limits exposure
duration rather than damage per retrieval. Accordingly, the
protocol controls unvetted-visibility duration; it does not solve
poisoning detection. Hard gates assume an honest control
plane; post-ﬁltering requires over-fetch; distributed clocks and
rollback remain out of scope.
D1 is one recipe-speciﬁc detector evaluated on 512 held-out
source groups. Its matched-recipe and cross-attack results do
not establish detector generality, unknown-attack robustness
or second-detector replication, and ofﬂine replay excludes
inference contention. The real-text study ends at retrieval
rather than answer generation. Physical-purge latency, storage
overhead while hidden vectors remain in the index, and restore
or reindex behavior were not evaluated.
The Standalone propagation panel is a single-run measure-
ment of the in-index update path; a second-host replication
passed its ﬁxed stability gate in only two of ﬁve runs and there-
fore contributes no latency estimate. The ﬁve HNSW runs are
single-node measurements, and 98,248 of 100,000 vectors are
deterministic pressure data. Requests are not independent sta-
tistical units; QPS and latency tails do not establish production
capacity, availability, fault tolerance, or distributed scaling.
Milvus Lite and cross-backend results validate implementation
consistency, not independent performance replication.
X. C ONCLUSION
Continuous RAG ingestion creates distinct unvetted- and
poisoning-exposure intervals. The protocol bounds the ﬁrst by
a deadline plus query-path enforcement delay and supports
lineage-scoped containment; on encoded natural-language
workloads under backlog it cut poisoned retrievals and
displaced clean results by roughly a factor of ﬁve, while
clean availability could lapse. D1’s false promotions and
refusals show why the poison bound is conditional and why
detector quality has a clean-content cost. Five single-node
HNSW runs show high-recall ANN retrieval under concurrent
ingestion for this workload.

manuscripts, veriﬁed the reported results and citations, and
take responsibility for the ﬁnal text.

title: Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
abstract: Agentic AI is emerging as a promising paradigm for automating complex cybersecurity decisions, yet its use in enforcing zero trust introduces significant challenges in safety, reliability, and policy compliance. This paper presents Agentic AI based zero trust architecture (Agentic-ZTA) that operationalizes the NIST SP 800-207 ZTA architecture control loop through coordinated multi- agent decision pipeline. In the proposed framework, policy knowledge is embedded into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and retrieved at inference time as top-k relevant policies. Access requests are intercepted by the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), enriched with contextual metadata. The request context is routed to a policy engine agent which invokes domain-specialized core agents first followed by supporting agents, if further evaluation needed. AI agents reason over access context, policy constraints and determine trust. The retrieved policies are embedded into agent prompt during inference time and agentic trust scores are aggregated and evaluated by a trust-algorithm, producing the final access decision for enforcement under continuous verification. We implement Agentic-ZTA in a testbed and evaluate it on representative access-control use cases scenarios. Our Agentic-ZTA framework achieves 95.0% accuracy, 93.9% precision, and 96.3% recall, and demonstrate the feasibility of enforcing zero trust using AI agents.

Agentic-ZTA: A Multi-Agent Architecture for
Autonomous Zero Trust Enforcement
Shovan Roya, Lopamudra Praharajb, Maanak Guptaa, Bhavani Thuraisinghamc
aDepartment of Computer Science, Tennessee Tech University, Cookeville, TN, USA
bDepartment of Computer Science, University of North Carolina Pembroke, Pembroke, NC, USA
cDepartment of Computer Science, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas, USA
Abstract
Agentic AI is emerging as a promising paradigm for automating complex cybersecurity decisions, yet its use in enforcing zero
trust introduces significant challenges in safety, reliability, and policy compliance. This paper presents Agentic AI based zero trust
architecture (Agentic-ZTA) that operationalizes the NIST SP 800-207 ZTA architecture control loop through coordinated multi-
agent decision pipeline. In the proposed framework, policy knowledge is embedded into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline
and retrieved at inference time as top-k relevant policies. Access requests are intercepted by the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP),
enriched with contextual metadata. The request context is routed to a policy engine agent which invokes domain-specialized core
agents first followed by supporting agents, if further evaluation needed. AI agents reason over access context, policy constraints
and determine trust. The retrieved policies are embedded into agent prompt during inference time and agentic trust scores are
aggregated and evaluated by a trust-algorithm, producing the final access decision for enforcement under continuous verification.
We implement Agentic-ZTA in a testbed and evaluate it on representative access-control use cases scenarios. Our Agentic-ZTA
framework achieves 95.0% accuracy, 93.9% precision, and 96.3% recall, and demonstrate the feasibility of enforcing zero trust
using AI agents.
Keywords:Agentic AI, Zero Trust Architecture, Internet of Battlefield Things, Multi-agent Systems, Retrieval-Augmented
Generation, Access Control
1. Introduction and Motivation
Zero trust architecture (ZTA) [1] is an approach to cyberse-
curity based on the principle “never trust, always verify”. It
is intended to remove the implicit trust in users, services, and
devices based only on their network location, affiliation, and
ownership. Zero trust focuses on protecting resources (e.g.,
devices, services, workflows, network accounts) through least
privilege, fine grained access control and dynamic policy up-
date [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. ZTA enforces secure authorized access to
enterprise resources while continually inspecting, monitoring,
and logging interactions with users, devices, applications, and
data across networks and workloads[7]. To realize these princi-
ples in practice, NIST defines a set of logical components that
collectively evaluate, authorize, and enforce access requests.
According to the NIST SP 800-207 [1], Zero Trust Architec-
ture is composed of three logical components: the Policy Deci-
sion Point (PDP), the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), and the
Policy Information Point (PIP). The PDP serves as the central
decision making component and determines whether to allow
or deny a request. Specifically, its Policy Engine (PE) evaluates
requests against defined policies, contextual telemetry, and trust
Email addresses:sroy42@tntech.edu(Shovan Roy),
lopamudra.praharaj@uncp.edu(Lopamudra Praharaj),
mgupta@tntech.edu(Maanak Gupta),
bhavani.thuraisingham@utdallas.edu(Bhavani Thuraisingham)
attributes. The PEP acts as the enforcement mechanism posi-
tioned between the subject and the resource. All access requests
pass through the PEP, which communicates with the PDP for an
authorization decision before allowing, denying or terminating
a session. PIPs serve as supporting data sources that supply the
PDP with real-time contextual and security telemetry required
for informed evaluations. These sources include identity man-
agement systems, compliance, Public Key Infrastructure (PKI),
threat intelligence platforms, Security Information and Event
Management (SIEM) systems, data access policies, Continu-
ous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) systems, and network
and activity logs. Collectively, these components enable ZTA
to continuously evaluate access requests based on identity, de-
vice posture, security context, and enterprise policies [1].
Prior to the adoption of Zero Trust, traditional cybersecu-
rity architectures primarily relied on perimeter-based security,
where users and devices located within the organizational net-
work were implicitly trusted. Access decisions were largely
based on network location, IP addresses, or predefined secu-
rity zones. However, with the explosion of cloud computing
and hybrid work, the perimeter no longer exists. Corporate data
no longer sits in a single physical data center. Employees ac-
cess company resources from home networks, coffee shops, and
personal devices, meaning there is no longer a clear "inside" to
protect. Zero Trust is essential because it secures access re-
gardless of location, device, or network, making it the viable
arXiv:2610.05782v1  [cs.AI]  5 Oct 2026
model for today’s complex, distributed IT ecosystems. Zero
Trust replaces implicit trust with continuous verification and
least-privilege access.
The use of machine learning (ML) in ZTA has significantly
expedited cybersecurity tasks such as detection of network in-
trusion, malware, phishing, anomaly detection, identification of
unusual network traffic and log analysis [8, 9, 10]. ML algo-
rithms leverage historical data to detect patterns that may in-
dicate potential security breaches [4]. Machine learning based
access control systems ranging from simple classifiers such as
SVMs[11] and random forests[12, 13] to deep learning like
DLBAC [14] replace manual policy rules to make allow/deny
decisions[15]. However, these approaches operate as black
boxes: they lack the reasoning needed to understand why an
event occurs. As a result, they fail to provide human-readable
justifications or explainable rationales for their decisions, mak-
ing it difficult to audit them in Zero Trust environments.
Large language models are increasingly used to make access
control decisions directly rather than only mining or generating
policies. Rubio-Medrano et al. pair LLMs with formal pol-
icy specifications so that access decisions remain traceable[16].
Cheng et al. propose LACE, a retrieval-augmented framework
where an LLM reasons over relevant policy context to deter-
mine IoT access decisions[17]. Similarly, Zisad and Hasan fine-
tune a Mistral 7B model to unify RBAC, ABAC, and DAC into
a single LLM-based decision layer [18]. However, these sys-
tems stop at the decision itself: they output allow/deny with an
explanation, but no subsequent mechanism auto-enforces that
decision, revokes access if conditions change, or re-validates
the session while it remains active which goes against Zero
Trust’s principle of continuous verification [1]. Nonetheless,
Zero trust enforcement based on LLM misses the autonomous
characteristics, i.e. it cannot initiate action independently and
cannot coordinate complex, multi-step process without human
interaction [19, 20]. To the best of our knowledge there is cur-
rently no framework that integrate Agentic AI into the Policy
Decision Point (PDP) which can autonomously enforce Zero
Trust access control decision.
Agentic AI, is the artificial intelligence systems that can au-
tonomously make decisions and take actions to pursue complex
goals with minimum or no human intervention [21, 22, 23, 24].
Agentic AI is used in Zero Trust access control to support con-
tinuous trust evaluation, context-aware authorization, and au-
tonomous response. It can analyze identity, device posture, be-
havioral, and environmental signals and initiate actions such
as privilege reduction, token revocation, or device isolation.
These capabilities improve least-privilege enforcement, threat
response, policy adaptation, and scalability in dynamic envi-
ronments such as Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT)[25] ,
where heterogeneous devices, changing mission conditions, in-
termittent connectivity, and evolving cyber threats require rapid
and adaptive access-control decisions. In addition, Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) [26] can reduce hallucinations
and reliance on obsolete policy information by grounding the
LLM’s responses in a retrievable and verifiable knowledge
base. This retrieved policy specific context generate more ac-
curate and up-to-date authorization decision. Upon reaching an

This paper is motivated by three foundational research ques-
tions:
•RQ1:Can LLM-based AI agents autonomously enforce a
NIST Zero Trust requirements and policies with sufficient
accuracy?
•RQ2:Can LLM-based agents produce decisions that are
auditable and accountable enough to trust the autonomous
enforcement?
•RQ3:Is the inference latency introduced by multi-agent
orchestration low enough to permit real-time Zero Trust
enforcement without degrading decision accuracy?
Table 1 compares the most closely related prior work across
six capability dimensions relevant to autonomous zero-trust en-
forcement, rating each as full support (+), partial support (◦),
or no support (–). The comparison reveals four compound lim-
itations that no single prior system addresses simultaneously.
L1:Static Policy Evaluation:All surveyed ZTA systems op-
erate with static policy rules. No system dynamically syn-
thesizes enforceable policies at inference time. Novel or
composite attack patterns therefore evade detection until
the policy base is manually updated.
L2:Ungrounded LLM Reasoning:Prior work that support
LLM generated reasoning but no way to check the reason-
ing behind it. None of these systems ground the model’s
reasoning from a policy knowledge base, so the LLM can
produce a response that sounds reasonable but has no real
evidence behind it.
L3:Lake of Autonomous Action:LLM-based systems pro-
duce detection or classification outputs but do not enforce
action autonomously. The resulting architectures require a
human analyst or a separate, manually configured enforce-
ment system to translate decision into PEP actions.
L4:Lack of Implementation:Most reviewed systems present
conceptual frameworks or partial prototypes without
2
demonstrating a working implementation. Only three
works [2, 7, 29] report partial implementations, and none
deploy a complete autonomous ZTA pipeline integrating
multi-agent orchestration, RAG-grounded reasoning, and
continuous validation.
This paper addresses all four limitations, as it integrates a
NIST-aligned PDP-PEP enforcement loop with multiple agents.
It takes decisions and autonomously enforce them (L1andL3).
It grounds each agent’s reasoning in RAG-retrieved policy ev-
idence (L2), and is validated through the implementation on a
testbed (L4). The key contributions to this work are as follows:
1. We introduce Agentic-ZTA, a conceptual framework that
reshapes NIST Zero Trust enforcement with autonomous
AI agents. Our framework use multi-agent system (MAS),
where some agents act as a core agent and some agents as
a supporting agent to enforce zero trust access control.
2. We develop a score-based trust algorithm (TA) that re-
ceives input from the agents in the form of either a trust
score or a threat score and produces a final trust score used
to reach the final access control decision.
3. We developed the sample prompt logic for the nine agents
- PE, IAM, PKI, Threat Detection, Compliance, CDM,
Activity and Log, Data Access Policy, SIEM.
4. We showcase the practical application of our proposed
framework using specific use cases, how our approach can
effectively enforce access control utilizing AI agents.
Section 2 reviews background and related work. Section 3
presents the Agentic Zero Trust architecture and agentic access
control workflow. Section 4 formalizes the trust algorithm. Sec-
tion 5 describes the deployment and use case scenarios. Sec-
tion 6 reports the experimental evaluation. Section 7 discusses
future research. Section 8 concludes.
2. Background and Related Work
2.1. Zero Trust Architecture
Zero trust architecture (ZTA) [1] is an approach to cyberse-
curity based on the principle “never trust, always verify”. Its
intended to remove the implicit trust in users, services, and
devices based only on their network location, affiliation, and
ownership. Zero trust focuses on protecting resources (e.g.,
devices, services, workflows, network accounts) through least
privilege, per-session basis fine grained access control and dy-
namic policy update [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. ZTA enforce risk-based
access controls while continually inspect, monitor, and log in-
teractions [7]. According to NIST ZTA, there are some core
components including the policy engine which evaluates access
requests using a trust algorithm, policy administrator translate
decision into enforceable actions. Supporting sources such as
identity systems, threat intelligence, SIEM, network and activ-
ity logs provide real time inputs to determine access decisions.
Consequently, ZTA has become the dominant access-control
paradigm for enterprise, cloud, and operational environments,
codified in U.S. federal policy and adopted across regulated
industries[1, 30, 31]. Its core requirement is: every access re-
quest must be authenticated, authorized, and continuously re-
evaluated through a Policy Decision Point (PDP) and Policy
Enforcement Point (PEP) control loop, with no trust granted
implicitly on the basis of network location or prior authoriza-
tion state[1].
2.2. ML Based Access Decision
A growing body of work replaces language-based access
control policies with trained ML models for access control
decision making, rather than using ML to assist policy min-
ing, verification, testing administration, monitoring and audit-
ing [15]. Nobi et al.[15] survey this line of work under the name
ML-based access control (MLBAC). Chang et al. proposed
a time-constrained access control system using SVMs trained
on login-time and password features to classify users and grant
access [11]. Outchakoucht et al. combined blockchain-based
policy management with reinforcement learning to dynami-
cally adjust IoT access control policies [32]. Cappelletti et
al. compared symbolic (decision tree, random forest) and
non-symbolic (support vector classifier, multi-layer perceptron)
ML for inferring ABAC access decisions from access logs[33].
Similarly, Khilar et al. evaluated an ensemble of random for-
est andk-nearest-neighbor classifiers for trust-based cloud re-
source access decisions[13], and Srivastava et al. proposed a
risk-adaptive access control framework using neural networks
and random forests to assess requester genuineness[34]. Liu
et al. improved the ABAC policy decision point directly with
a random-forest-based permission decision engine[12], while
Karimi et al. applied reinforcement learning to adaptive ABAC
policy learning under sparse-log conditions[35]. Deep Learn-
ing Based Access Control (DLBAC) replaces attribute and pol-
icy engineering with a ResNet-based neural network trained
directly on user and resource metadata[14]. Notably, none
of these access-decision approaches employ large language
models. The use of LLM-based agents for zero trust access
decision-making extends this line of work beyond the classical
and deep-learning methods.
2.3. Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Policy Grounding
Lewis et al.[26] demonstrated that augmenting LLM genera-
tion with differentiable retrieval substantially reduces hallucina-
tion, establishing RAG as a viable approach for security policy
grounding where factual accuracy is strictly required. However,
in their survey of LLM security vulnerabilities, Yao et al.[36]
identified non-reproducibility across invocations and hallucina-
tion under adversarial inputs as the primary failure modes in
auditable enforcement layers. Agentic-ZTA directly mitigates
these non-reproducibility risks through two deterministic mech-
anisms: fixed top-kvector retrieval over the policy knowledge
base and greedy decoding (temperature=0) across all agent
inference calls. This combination ensures that context retrieval
remains stable for identical inputs while eliminating stochastic
variance during policy evaluation.
3
2.4. Multi-Agent Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
Multi-agent systems (MAS) distribute reasoning and opera-
tional tasks across specialized autonomous agents, each main-
taining domain-specific operational contexts[27]. In cyber-
security, MAS architectures have been applied to intrusion
detection[37], network traffic classification, and automated in-
cident response. Early designs relied heavily on static rule
engines, which subsequent works replaced with reinforcement
learning (RL) and multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithms[29].
However, RL-based approaches exhibit critical drawbacks in
security-sensitive deployments: formulating well-calibrated re-
ward functions is challenging, sparse feedback delays training
convergence and learned policies frequently fail to generalize
against unseen attack scenarios[38, 39].
More recently, Deng et al.[28] surveyed vulnerabilities spe-
cific to LLM-driven agent deployments, identifying prompt
injection, knowledge-base poisoning, and orchestration-layer
hijacking as primary threat vectors. Agentic-ZTA miti-
gates knowledge-base poisoning and hallucination by enforcing
domain-specific, policy-grounded vector retrieval. Each agent’s
contextual inputs strictly to authoritative, verified telemetry.
Beyond reasoning quality, separation of duties constitutes a
foundational security rationale for multi-agent architectures. In
access control, no single autonomous component should pos-
sess unilateral authority to allow access, preserving an essential
principle first formalized in RBAC systems to prevent fraud and
single-point compromise[40, 41].
Agentic-ZTA enforces this separation directly within its or-
chestration workflow. Discrete operational checks including
identity verification (IAM), cryptographic validation (PKI), be-
havioral anomaly tracking (SIEM), and policy checkes (Data
Access Policy) are decoupled into specialized autonomous
agents, each grounded in its dedicated RAG pipeline. To en-
sure default deny policy, any core agentDENYverdict triggers
immediate enforcement by the PEP, bypassing subsequent trust
evaluation. In contrast, anALLOWverdict requires multi-agent
consensus through formal trust fusion. Consequently, a com-
promised agent can at worst result in a denial of service, but
can never unilaterally allow unauthorized access.
3. Architecture Overview
Agentic-ZTA (Fig.1) separates the control plane from the
data plane, adhering to the NIST SP 800-207 reference
architecture[1]. The control plane hosts the Policy Decision
Point (PDP), wherein the Policy Engine (PE) agent operates as
the central orchestrator. It does not itself hold domain knowl-
edge, identity records, certificates, threat signatures instead it
receives the access request, decides which agents to invoke, col-
lects their assessments and provides the final access decision
applying trust algorithm. We structure the evaluation agents
into two tiers based on decision authority:core agentsandsup-
porting agents.
Acore agentpossesses authoritative power: a negative as-
sessment terminates the agentic evaluation immediately, abort-
ing further agent queries and bypassing trust algorithm. The
Identity Management (IAM) Agent,Threat Detection Agent, and
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Agentserve as core agents.
They map to the identity, credential, and threat dimensions
that NIST designates as non-negotiable trust primitives for any
PDP[1]. If any of the core agents decides on aDENY, the PE
agent instructs the PEP to enforce an immediate denial action.
Conversely, asupporting agentprovides auxiliary contextual
telemetry such as compliance posture, policy fit or log anoma-
lies that feeds into the confidence-weighted trust score, but its
output alone cannot unilaterally force aDENY. TheData Ac-
cess Policy Agent,Security Information and Event Management
(SIEM) Agent,Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM)
Agent,Compliance Agent, andActivity and Log Monitoring
Agentconstitute this tier. Supporting agents are invoked only
when all core agents have issued anALLOW.
The data plane hosts the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP),
which mediates all communication between the subject and the
protected resources. The user resides in theuntrusted zonei.e.
no request is trusted. The PEP shields the resources blocking
all traffic until the control plane (PDP) evaluates the request.
Once the PE Agent returns an ALLOW decision, the PEP grants
ephemeral access strictly to the requested endpoint under gran-
ular micro-segmentation, preserving strict isolation between re-
sources. While access remains active, the PE Agent continu-
ously re-evaluates the session and revokes access through the
PEP if an anomaly is detected.
The operational workflow has been explain in details in sec-
tion 3.2. A continuous validation loop operates concurrently
with this workflow. Throughout an active session, the PE agent
periodically re-evaluates trust attributes using real-time inputs
from both core and supporting agents, ensuring persistent com-
pliance rather than relying on a static, one-time check.
3.1. Agent Description and Sample Prompt
3.1.1. Orchestrator Agent:
Policy Engine (PE) Agent: The PE Agent is the principal

pute a confidence-weighted trust scoreT, which is compared
against the destination zone’s trust thresholdτ z to reach a fi-
nal ALLOW or DENY decision. The PE Agent utilizes AI-
based reasoning to contextualize heterogeneous agent outputs
and synthesize them into a single, auditable decision, ensur-

3.2. Agentic-ZTA Access Control Workflow
The Agentic-ZTA architecture Fig-1 implements the NIST
SP 800-207 PDP/PEP control loop as a multi-agent pipeline,
coordinating core and supporting agents under the PE agent or-
chestrator before the PEP enforces the resulting decision. Fig.2
demonstrates access request workflow from submission to en-
forcement.
1. A subject submits a request carrying user, device and re-
source information to the PEP.
2. The PEP intercepts the request and constructs a normal-
ized access request by appending context (session, device,
user and certificate metadata).
3. The policies are embedded with a sentence transformer,
stored in separate vector databases and the top-kmatching
policies are retrieved by the agent during their inference
time.
4. Access request is sent to the PE agent for evaluation.
5. The PE agent extracts the access-request context from the
prompt and parallel invokes the core agent(s).
6. Each invoked agent retrieves Top-k matching policies from
the vector database and generates a structured response
(action- DENY/ALLOW, trust score, confidence score,
reasoning).
7. If any core agent issues a DENY, the PEP enforces the
decision and the request path terminates at Step 9 without
invoking supporting agents.
8. Otherwise, when all core agents issue Allow, the PE agent
parallel invokes the supporting agent(s), which retrieves
Top-k matching policies from the vector database and gen-
erate structured responses. The core and supporting agent
responses are then jointly aggregated and evaluated by the
trust algorithm (Algorithm 1).
9. The PEP enforces the resulting decision: on ALLOW,
the session is created and resource access is granted. On
DENY, the session is terminated and access is revoked.
10. Under continuous verification, a change in policy or con-
text triggers re-evaluation from Step 2 without requiring a
new subject-initiated request.
4. Trust Algorithm
The PE Agent receives an independent assessment from each
invoked agent, and these assessments can differ in score and
confidence. A trust algorithm converts them into one auditable
ALLOW or DENY decision. It addresses three needs. First, it
gives the PE Agent a deterministic, reproducible fusion step,

Second, it weights each assessment by the agent’s stated confi-

5. Use Cases Scenarios
5.1. IoBT Scenario Context
The scenario in Figure 3 reflects an Internet of Battlefield
Things (IoBT), a heterogeneous environment in which a wide
range of sensors, devices, vehicles, soldier wearables, and com-
mand systems collaborate to accomplish mission objectives un-
der contested conditions [45, 25]. In IoBT coalition operation
multiple nations and partners share battlefield information to
accomplish mission goal while still protecting their own secu-
rity rules, data classifications.
The testbed models five zones:Nation A Tactical,Nation B
Tactical,Mission HQ,Mission Partner, and a centralShared
Data Fabricthat serves as the coalition exchange hub.
Nation A Tactical networkrepresents one nation’s frontline
battlefield enclave. It contains heterogeneous edge devices such
as unmanned aerial vehicles (UA Vs), unattended ground sen-
sors (UGS), unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and soldier
wearables, along with edge processor, MQTT hub and Com-
mand and Control (C2) server. These devices constantly gen-
erate telemetry such as position, health status, reconnaissance
feeds and mission alerts. Raw battlefield data is first collected
here. These devices often operate with limited bandwidth, low
energy, and limited connectivity. The MQTT broker supports
local communication among devices, the edge processor per-
forms initial preprocessing and filtering, and the C2 server in-
tegrates the resulting data before publishing the consolidated
information to the shared data fabric.
Nation B Tacticalis a separate sovereign tactical enclave with
a similar structure, but its own policies, priorities, and trust
rules. Even though it participates in the same coalition mission,
it does not automatically trust other zones or accept access re-
quests. This is because coalition partners may have different
kinds of intelligence, but each nation still has to decide what
can be shared, what must remain local, and what requires extra
protection.
Mission HQacts as the coalition command and intelligence
center. It receives consolidated telemetry from the tactical
zones, fuses the data into a broader mission picture and sends
mission commands back to tactical operators. Mission HQ
must make sure that the information it receives is trusted and
that the commands it sends stay within mission and policy
boundary.
Mission Partnerrepresents allied or coalition partner forces
that support the mission but may not have the same level of ac-
cess as the tactical zones- Nation A and Nation B. These nodes
are allowed to receive processed intelligence that is relevant to
their assigned tasks, but raw sensor telemetry is still controlled
by coalition releasability rules. Coalition data sharing is selec-
tive, conditional, and based on mission need.
TheShared Data Fabricis the central exchange point that
connects all of the zones. It is not just a storage layer or a data
relay. In this architecture, it is the place where coalition data
is checked, filtered, and controlled before being shared across
boundaries. All inter-zone traffic passes through this fabric, and
the exchange happens over HTTPS so that communication re-
mains protected while still allowing controlled sharing.
Thousands of requests may arrive from sensors, vehicles,
operators, commanders, and coalition partners. Each request
may depend on the current mission phase, device health, net-
work condition, and threat level. A rule-based system alone is
too rigid for this environment because it cannot adapt quickly
enough when devices move, credentials are compromised, or a
mission priority suddenly changes. In this scenario Agentic-
ZTA is necessary: it gives the system an autonomous deci-
sion layer that can continuously evaluate who is requesting,
what they want, whether the device or user is trustworthy, and
whether the request fits the current mission and coalition policy.
Agentic-ZTA system is deployed at the Shared Data Fabric.
Each zone’s gateway acts as a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)
that intercepts every access request, add metadata and forwards
it to the Policy Engine (PE) Agent for decision.

setting, we deployed 5 zoned IoBT testbed across Linux virtual

6.2. Agent Development
All experiments were executed in a Linux environment using
a self-hosted Ollama endpoint. Ollama was installed and run
locally on the testbed machine, serving the LLM (Llama 3.1)
over a local endpoint. The current implementation uses a single
shared LLM backend for all agents rather than separate mod-
els or per-agent instances. Specialization is achieved through
agent-specific prompts, tool bindings, and isolated ChromaDB
policy collections. Policies are stored in per-agent collec-
tions forIAM,PKI,Threat Detection,CDM,Data Access
Policy,SIEM, andActivity and Logs Monitoring. Each
agent retrieves up to the top-5 matching rules from its own col-
lection during inference.
The PE agent evaluates the invoked core agents first and ter-
minates immediately if any core agent returnsDENY. If all core
agents allow the request, the supporting agents are invoked in
parallel. Orchestration is implemented with Python’sasyncio
for concurrency, while blocking RAG retrieval and model calls
are isolated withasyncio.to_thread(), so that core and sup-
porting agents can run concurrently against the single shared
model without requiring separate model instances.
6.3. Dataset Generation
To evaluate the proposed zero-trust access-control frame-
work under controlled and repeatable conditions, we con-
structed a synthetic dataset of 160 access requests. The dataset
was designed to capture both allowable access request and de-
niable access request.
The dataset was organized into four equally sized groups.
The first group contains 40 fully compliant requests. These
requests use valid certificates, Secret-level clearance, verified
multi-factor authentication, single concurrent session, verified
firmware integrity, no configuration drift, and current patch sta-
tus. The second group contains additional 40 compliant re-
quests with the same access request characteristics. These two
groups provide 80 samples and expectedALLOWrequests.
The remaining 80 records represent deniable conditions.
The third group contains 40 requests with identity and device
anomaly evidences. The fourth group contains 40 requests
exhibiting compromised or degraded device posture. These
samples include configuration drift, outdated patches, unknown
firmware integrity, reduced clearance, multiple concurrent ses-
sions, and failed MFA verification.
Contextual fields included the source IP address, source
zone, destination IP address, destination zone, access mode,
protocol, and MQTT topic. Identity and authorization fields
included certificate validity, clearance level, MFA status, role,
and explicitly granted permissions. Session-related fields in-
cluded the session identifier, concurrent-session count and re-
cent anomaly count. Device-posture fields captured firmware
integrity, configuration drift, and patch status.
The dataset is balanced with 80 compliant and 80 non-
compliant requests.

6.6. Comparison with Rule-Based Access Control
To contextualize Agentic-ZTA’s decision quality and latency,
we additionally implemented a deterministic, rule-based evalu-
ator for the same access-control policies. The rule-based eval-
uator applies the identical policy set as IF-THEN conditionals
without LLM inference or retrieval.

exceeds 2 minutes when both the core and supporting phases
are invoked, since agents within a phase run concurrently but
the two phases execute sequentially. This latency is dominated
by model inference time rather than retrieval or orchestration

14
Although static rule-based access control may provide per-
fect accuracy on a finite rule set in less time, five reasons mo-
tivate agentic access control over it: (1) automation, (2) au-
tonomous decision-making, (3) contextual explanations for op-
erators, (4) the ability to address novel threats, and (5) faster
policy adaptation.
Automation:A rule-based evaluator only executes condi-
tionals that an administrator has already authored. Every new
policy requires manual rule-writing before the system can act
on it. In Agentic-ZTA, agents evaluate access requests against
retrieved policy and threat evidence without requiring a human,
removing this manual step from the access-control loop.
Autonomous decision-making:A rule-based access control
only returns the outcome of a fixed conditional that an admin-
istrator has already authored, it does not decide anything on its
own. In Agentic-ZTA agents reason over request context, re-
trieved policy, and threat evidence at inference time and reach
an access decision autonomously, without a human.
Contextual explanations for operators:LLM-based agents
can translate security evidence into understandable natural-
language reasoning, reducing analyst investigation effort and
improving decision transparency [46]. Agentic-ZTA records
each agent’sreasoningalong with rule identifiers, preserving
rule-level auditability while providing an interpretable justifica-
tion.
Static rules have limited ability to address novel threats:
Rule-based access control systems can detect only conditions
explicitly represented in their policies. When a new attack pat-
tern appears, the system stays exposed until an administrator
writes and deploys a new rule for it [47]. Agentc-ZTA can as-
sess the semantic context of a request using retrieved policy and
threat evidence, enabling risk assessment that was not present
in predefined rules.
Policy adaptation can be faster:Updating a rule-based
system requires administrators to author, test, and deploy new
rules for each policy or threat change. In Agentic-ZTA, RAG-
grounded agents retrieve updated policy and threat knowledge
from the knowledge base at inference time. Knowledge-base
update can influence subsequent assessments without modify-
ing agent code or redeploying the orchestration layer.

7. Discussion and Future Research
7.1. Discussion
Agentic-ZTA enforced the default-deny policy without hu-
man intervention, achieving 95.0% accuracy, 93.9% precision,
96.3% recall, and a 95.1% F1-score on the 160-request eval-
uation set (Section 6.4). The PE Agent executed enforcement
tools on both ALLOW and DENY outcomes. The deterministic
rule-based baseline reached 100% accuracy on the same set, so
the benefit of the proposed framework is autonomous decision-
making without administrator-authored rules, not higher accu-
racy.
Each decision carried the agent rationales, the trust score
T(when computed), and the identifier of the retrieved policy
rule, which makes individual decisions traceable. The core-
agent DENY and the fail-safe default ensure that a compro-
mised agent can block access but cannot allow it alone. Repro-
ducibility across repeated runs was not measured and remains a
limitation, because LLM inference is non-deterministic.
The main cost is latency. On CPU-only hardware, single-
request latency ranged from 45.67 s to 134.32 s, compared with
0.7 ms for the rule-based evaluator (Section 6.5). Throughput
stayed below 1 req/min at all tested concurrency levels. The
current prototype therefore does not support real-time enforce-
ment.
7.2. Limitations and Future Research
The following limitations bound the scope of our findings
and point to directions for future work.
Single shared model backend.All eight agents use
one shared local LLM (llama3.1served via Ollama) rather
than separate, domain-specialized models. Specialization is
achieved only through agent-specific prompts, tool bindings,
and isolated ChromaDB collections. Future work should eval-
uate quantized models per agent under an asynchronous multi-
model deployment to determine whether accuracy and latency
improve.
Adversarial robustness.This study does not evaluate di-
rect or indirect prompt injection, jailbreaking, task drift, mem-
ory poisoning, or other adversarial-input attacks. Because each
agent ingests retrieved policy text and request metadata directly
into its prompt, resistance to crafted input and retrieval poison-
ing remains an open question. A dedicated adversarial stress
test is needed to establish robustness empirically.
CPU-only inference and latency.The testbed runs with-
out GPU acceleration, and the measured latency is likely at-
tributable in large part to this constraint. GPU inference is
expected to reduce latency substantially, but this has not been
tested. Future work should measure end-to-end latency under
GPU inference and with smaller per-agent models.
Simulated testbed.All results were collected in a simulated
five-zone IoBT coalition testbed on a synthetic dataset, not on
a live operational network. Behavior under real network con-
ditions, such as packet loss, adversarial jamming, or genuine
multi-nation policy conflicts, has not been evaluated.
8. Conclusion
This paper proposes Agentic-ZTA, a multi-agent RAG-
enabled framework that operationalizes the NIST SP 800-
207 PDP/PEP control loop through autonomous, domain-
specialized LLM agents. Trust evaluation is decomposed across
agents: core agents are evaluated first, and a DENY from
any core agent is enforced directly by the PEP without wait-
ing for further agents or running trust fusion. When all core
agents return ALLOW, supporting-agent assessments are com-
bined through confidence-weighted trust fusion, so decisions
are grounded in retrievable policy evidence rather than static
rules.
The IoBT testbed demonstrated that the framework can sup-
port diverse access-control outcomes with clear provenance.
A compliant cross-zone write was permitted when all invoked
agents converged above the trust threshold. A compromised-
insider read was blocked directly by a core agent’s DENY on
cloned-credential evidence, without invoking trust fusion. An
over-privileged cross-zone read was denied through trust fusion
when the combined score fell below the acceptance threshold.
Importantly, when releasability policy changed in the retrieved
knowledge base, the corresponding access decision changed
without retraining or redeployment, showing that the system
can adapt to policy updates at runtime.
Overall, the findings suggest that multi-agent LLM orches-
tration, when coupled with retrieval-grounded policy knowl-
edge, provides a practical and transparent mechanism for Zero
Trust enforcement in highly dynamic and adversarial settings.

title: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
abstract: Formal specifications are essential for deductive program verification, providing semantic abstractions for compositional verification of complex software. However, manually constructing specifications is labor-intensive, motivating automated synthesis. Despite recent advances in large language models (LLMs), existing approaches often rely on forward-only workflows and localized repair, limiting their effectiveness on real-world programs with complex dependencies among functions and loops. Verification failures may stem from previously generated specifications, causing cascading failures that local refinement cannot resolve. To address these challenges, we present SpecAgent, an agentic framework for synthesizing high-quality ACSL specifications for real-world C programs. SpecAgent integrates four components: dependency-aware planning to identify specification targets, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide relevant specification patterns and program context, agentic repair to diagnose defects and revisit dependent specifications, and agentic critique to assess and refine semantic strength beyond proof success. We evaluate SpecAgent on specification synthesis and program verification tasks. On 50 programs from 14 real-world repositories, SpecAgent with DeepSeek-V4 achieves 96.82% precision and 88.95% recall in synthesizing correct and strong specifications, outperforming all baselines. On 811 real-world verification targets, it successfully discharges 604, also surpassing existing baselines. These results demonstrate SpecAgent's effectiveness in synthesizing high-quality specifications and facilitating real-world program verification.

SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic
Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
LEZHI MA,Nanjing University, China
HAN WANG,Nanjing University, China
SHANGQING LIU,Nanjing University, China
JIAWAN WANG,Nanjing University, China
LEI BU,Nanjing University, China
Formal specifications are essential for deductive program verification, as they provide semantic abstractions
that enable compositional verification on complex software systems. The difficulties in manually constructing
such specifications gave birth to automated specification synthesis, and recent advances in relevant approaches
based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promising capabilities. Nevertheless, existing approaches
often follow a forward-only synthesis workflow and rely on localized repair strategies, which limit their
effectiveness on real-world programs with complex dependencies among functions and loops. In such scenarios,
verification failures may originate from previously generated specifications rather than the immediate failure
locations, leading to cascading failures that cannot be effectively addressed by local refinement.
In this paper, we presentSpecAgent, an agentic framework for synthesizing high-quality ACSL specifications
for real-world C programs.SpecAgentintegrates four complementary components into a unified workflow: it
analyzes program structures and dependencies to plan specification targets, leverages retrieval-augmented
generation with a specification knowledge base to provide LLMs with relevant specification patterns and
program context, employs agentic repairing to diagnose specification defects and revisit previously generated
specifications when verification failures are traced to their dependencies, and applies an agentic critique
mechanism to assess and refine semantic strength beyond proof success. We extensively evaluateSpecAgent
on both specification synthesis and program verification tasks. On a benchmark consisting of 50 programs
from 14 real-world repositories,SpecAgentwith DeepSeek-V4 achieves 96.82% precision and 88.95% recall
in synthesizing correct yet strong specifications, substantially outperforming all baselines including Codex
equipped with GPT-5.6. We further evaluateSpecAgenton 811 real-world verification targets, whereSpecAgent
successfully discharges 604 targets, surpassing existing baselines. The results show thatSpecAgentcan
effectively synthesize high-quality specifications and facilitate verification of real-world software.
1 Introduction
Program verification [25] is an essential technique for software reliability assurance, which can
provide rigorous guarantees by proving consistency between the target program and given proper-
ties (including functional correctness and runtime safety constraints), complementing conventional
techniques such as software testing [ 27]. However, automatically verifying complex programs
against high-level properties is fundamentally challenging, as the general program verification
problem is undecidable [35] due to the potential unbounded behaviors produced by intricate pro-
gram structures such as loops and function calls. One typical approach to achieving deductive
verification is based onauxiliary specifications[ 20], which are expressed in parsable, unambiguous
formal languages and can abstract the behaviors of individual program structures. Specifically,
loop invariants summarize the properties preserved across loop iterations, while function contracts
(typically including preconditions and postconditions) characterize the behavioral guarantees of
function calls. These specifications provide the semantic abstractions needed by the verifier to
